meta.blurb: Amara is fourteen, and her science project has one rule. Show the evidence. With her grandfather Kofi, a retired cook, she tests the big claims about food and builds a plate of everyday foods that may help the body look after itself.
meta.bible: Amara: a schoolgirl of about fourteen who is choosing a science project; curious and sensible, and she likes to ask what the evidence is. Kofi: her grandfather, a retired Cook who ran a small restaurant; warm, funny and practical. Mrs Okoro: Amara's science teacher. The book runs over about eight weeks, from the day Amara picks her project to the school Science Fair, in Kofi's kitchen, the market and the school hall. The project is a Protection Plate: a plate of everyday foods that may help the body look after itself. Key ideas: the body already protects and repairs itself, through the Skin, the Immune system and the repair of cells; food supports these jobs but is not a cure; observational studies show links, not proof; trials give stronger evidence; the whole pattern of eating matters more than one Superfood. Foods: Berries, Anthocyanins; leafy greens, Vitamin K, Warfarin; Broccoli, Cabbage, Cruciferous vegetables; Tomatoes, Lycopene; Onions, Garlic; Beans, Lentils, Fibre; Oats, Beta-glucan, whole grains; Nuts; Olive oil; Oily fish, Omega-3; Yoghurt; Tea; Turmeric, Curcumin; Cocoa, Flavanols; frozen vegetables. A large Mediterranean diet trial in Spain found fewer heart problems in people given extra olive oil or nuts. The World Health Organization advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, free sugars under ten percent of energy, and under five grams of salt a day; its cancer agency in 2015 classed processed meat as a cause of bowel cancer and red meat as a probable one. Trials of high-dose Beta-carotene pills in people who smoked found more lung cancer, not less. Alcohol raises the risk of several cancers. Charred and burnt food can form harmful compounds. Safety facts: nut allergies can be serious; vitamin K foods matter to people who take warfarin; anyone with a health condition, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should ask a doctor or registered dietitian. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and a little funny; honest about uncertainty; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice. Added for the full-length book: Efua: Amara's mother, busy and practical, who works long hours. Kojo: Amara's little brother, two years old, a fussy eater. Zainab: Amara's best friend, whose Science Fair project is about drinking Water. Dev: a classmate whose project is on Supplements. Auntie Grace: sells fruit and vegetables at the Saturday Market. Mr Danso: Kofi's neighbour, who takes Warfarin. Mr Quaye: a neighbour who sells a Miracle juice. Ms Adebayo: a registered Dietitian at the local clinic. Dr Mensah: the visiting judge at the Science Fair, a man who is a nutrition researcher. The Evidence Ladder: Amara's five rungs, from Stories, to Lab studies, to Groups of people watched, to Trials, to Reviews of many trials. The Five Questions poster: who says it, how many people, what kind of study, how big is the effect, who gains. Amara's rule: Show the evidence. Kofi's rule: a kitchen rule must be tasted too. The Honest Science Prize: won at the Fair. Extra facts, all kept careful: James Lind, a ship's surgeon, in 1747 tried six remedies on twelve sailors with Scurvy; oranges and lemons worked best. Platelets and Fibrin make a clot; red blood cells last about four months. The top layer of Skin is replaced about every month. Vaccines train the Immune system. A red Pepper holds more Vitamin C than an Orange. Cabbage, Kale, Sprouts and Cauliflower are cruciferous; Glucosinolates and Sulforaphane are their sulphur compounds; Anthocyanins turn red cabbage juice pink with Lemon. Lycopene is released by cooking Tomatoes. Raw kidney beans are poisonous and must be boiled hard for at least ten minutes. Chickpeas, Pulses, Wholegrain, Barley, Millet and Brown rice are whole grains; fibre advice is about twenty-five to thirty grams a day. Gut Microbes feed on fibre. Peanuts, Walnuts, Almonds, Cashews; Sesame, Sunflower and Pumpkin seeds; a handful of nuts is about thirty grams; a nut allergy can be serious. In the Spanish trial, called Predimed, about seven thousand older adults at high risk of heart disease followed a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil or nuts, or were told to eat less fat; the first report was withdrawn and republished in 2018 after some people were found to have been assigned wrongly, and the result was similar. Salmon, Sardines, Mackerel, Herring and Trout are oily fish; Mercury is found in large fish such as Shark, Swordfish and Marlin. Fermented foods: Kimchi, Sauerkraut, Kefir, Ogi. Polyphenols; the World Health Organization's cancer agency says very hot drinks above sixty-five degrees probably cause cancer of the Oesophagus. Tea can block iron. Curcumin is poorly absorbed, helped a little by Black pepper; high-dose Turmeric pills have rarely harmed the Liver. Flavanols. Free sugars: under ten percent of energy, about twelve teaspoons a day on a diet of two thousand calories; a can of fizzy drink often holds about thirty-five grams, nine teaspoons. A trial in the Netherlands gave children sugary or sugar-free drinks for about eighteen months. Trials show sugar does not make children wild. The World Health Organization in 2023 advised against sweeteners for weight control. Sodium, Potassium; salt under five grams a day, about one level teaspoon; most salt comes from bread, soups, sauces and processed food. In 2015 a panel of experts from ten countries at the International Agency for Research on Cancer, called Iarc, placed processed meat in Group One, which means strong evidence and not equal danger, and red meat in Group Two A, probable. A small 2019 trial in a research ward: twenty adults ate about five hundred more calories a day on an Ultra-processed diet and gained about a kilogram. Nova groups foods by processing. Acrylamide forms in starchy food browned too far; aim for golden. Aflatoxin comes from Mould on stored groundnuts and grain. The World Health Organization says no level of alcohol is completely safe. Two trials in the 1990s, one in Finland and one in the United States, found Beta-carotene pills raised lung cancer in smokers. Vitamin A, Vitamin D, Vitamin E and Vitamin B12; Folic acid; St John's wort and Grapefruit can change how some medicines work. Superfood and Detox have no scientific meaning; the liver and kidneys already clear the body. Teenagers should move about an hour a day and sleep eight to ten hours; adults about two and a half hours of activity a week. Cooked rice must be cooled fast and kept in the Fridge. Kojo is two and may need ten tries to accept a new food. The Protection Plate in the end: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains, a quarter protein, plant oil, water, and a Keep Small corner for salt, sugar, processed meat and alcohol. Kofi stopped smoking twenty years ago. Setting in the end: school hall, Kofi's kitchen, the Saturday Market.

beats.scene: Amara reads a project sheet at the kitchen table while Kofi stirs a pot
beats.summary: Amara must choose a science project; any topic will do if the evidence is honest, and she picks food.

beats.scene: Kofi in a white apron holds a wooden spoon beside a bubbling pot
beats.summary: Her grandfather Kofi, a retired cook of thirty years, offers to help though he never studied what is in food.

beats.scene: Amara and Kofi stick yellow notes of food sayings on the fridge door
beats.summary: They list the food claims they have heard all their lives, from carrots for eyes to sugar making children wild.

beats.scene: Kofi opens an old restaurant notebook on a table crowded with sauce stains
beats.summary: Kofi remembers his regulars, who each swore by a different food for health.

beats.scene: Amara writes Show the evidence in big letters across the top of a page
beats.summary: Amara sets one rule for the project, and Kofi adds that a kitchen rule needs tasting too.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro leans on her desk and asks Amara what protect really means
beats.summary: Mrs Okoro makes Amara define her question: which everyday foods may help the body look after itself.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro writes good sources and weak sources in two columns on the board
beats.summary: Mrs Okoro explains where trustworthy evidence comes from, and why my uncle said does not count.

beats.scene: A paper calendar of eight weeks hangs on the fridge with magnets
beats.summary: Amara and Kofi plan eight weeks, from the body and the evidence to foods, a plan and the Science Fair.

beats.scene: Amara draws an empty plate on card and Kofi taps it with a spoon
beats.summary: Amara sketches the Protection Plate she hopes to fill, and Kofi vows to taste every test.

beats.scene: Amara lies awake in bed with a notebook open on the blanket
beats.summary: That night Amara writes her first question, and Kofi leaves a note saying to start with the body.

beats.scene: Kofi shows a long pale scar on his hand under the kitchen light
beats.summary: Kofi's kitchen scars lead Amara to ask how a cut heals itself.

beats.scene: A drop of blood on a finger becomes a dark scab under a magnifier
beats.summary: A cut closes first with a clot made of platelets and a net of protein.

beats.scene: Amara touches her own forearm skin beside a diagram of its layers
beats.summary: Skin is a shield against germs, and its top layer is replaced about every month.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro draws guard cells fighting germs on the whiteboard in coloured pens
beats.summary: The immune system has barriers, patrol cells and a memory, and vaccines train that memory.

beats.scene: A red blood cell diagram sits beside an x-ray of a mended arm bone
beats.summary: Cells are always being replaced or repaired, red blood cells last about four months, and bones knit.

beats.scene: A builder stacks bricks beside a blueprint labelled with food words
beats.summary: The body's repair work needs materials from food, such as protein, vitamin C and other nutrients.

beats.scene: A bottle of miracle juice stands next to a plain apple on a wall
beats.summary: Kofi's neighbour sells a miracle juice, and Amara writes that food supports the body but cures nothing.

beats.scene: Kofi sits alone on a porch step while Amara sits beside him
beats.summary: Some illness is bad luck, age or genes and not anyone's fault, so food gives no guarantee.

beats.scene: A tall glass of orange juice stands beside a short stack of coins
beats.summary: If you lack a nutrient food can fix it, but extra beyond what you need does little.

beats.scene: Amara types the first page of her report with Kofi's tea beside the screen
beats.summary: Amara writes that the body is the protector and food is the helper.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro points at a chart of two groups of people on a whiteboard
beats.summary: Scientists follow large groups of people to find links between food and health, but links are not proof.

beats.scene: An ice cream van and a sunburnt swimmer share one sunny beach scene
beats.summary: Two things can rise together because of a third, as with ice cream and sunburn.

beats.scene: Amara frowns at a blank food diary page with only Tuesday filled in
beats.summary: Studies of eating rely on memory, and Amara cannot remember what she ate last Tuesday.

beats.scene: Two soup pots with coloured labels stand in a row with a clipboard
beats.summary: In a trial, chance decides who eats what, and the groups are compared.

beats.scene: A wooden sailing ship at sea with twelve sailors and a surgeon below deck
beats.summary: In 1747 James Lind tested six remedies for scurvy on twelve sailors, and oranges and lemons worked best.

beats.scene: Amara looks at two identical glasses on a table with one marked in secret
beats.summary: Trials are hard because people cannot eat different food for years and hide it from themselves.

beats.scene: A petri dish with a drop of liquid glowing under a lab lamp
beats.summary: A substance that works in a dish or a mouse may do nothing in a person.

beats.scene: Amara pins a five-rung ladder of evidence on the kitchen wall
beats.summary: Amara builds a ladder of evidence from stories up to many trials combined.

beats.scene: Amara and Kofi read a loud newspaper headline about chocolate with a magnifying glass
beats.summary: They test a headline with questions: who, how many, what kind of study and how big.

beats.scene: A long family dinner table with many different dishes and no single star dish
beats.summary: The whole pattern of eating matters more than any single superfood.

beats.scene: Colourful stalls line a busy Saturday market while Amara and Kofi stop at one
beats.summary: At Auntie Grace's market stall they meet the rainbow of plants and the thousands of substances inside.

beats.scene: A bright pepper plant with a small caterpillar on a leaf in the sun
beats.summary: Plants make many substances to protect themselves, and some of these may help us too.

beats.scene: A plate of pale cauliflower, banana and white beans beside a coloured plate
beats.summary: Colour is a clue but not a rule, and pale foods like onions and cauliflower count too.

beats.scene: A kitchen scale holds a pile of vegetables weighing four hundred grams
beats.summary: The WHO advises at least four hundred grams of fruit and vegetables a day, about five portions.

beats.scene: Amara reads a bar chart of fruit and vegetable eaters beside a thick report
beats.summary: Large studies link more fruit and vegetables with lower risk of heart disease, though not as proof.

beats.scene: Red cabbage juice turns pink in a glass as Amara squeezes lemon into it
beats.summary: Amara boils red cabbage and sees anthocyanins change colour when she adds lemon.

beats.scene: Amara washes blueberries and strawberries in a white bowl at the sink
beats.summary: Berries are linked with a healthier heart and blood pressure, though the trials are small and the effect modest.

beats.scene: A bowl of cheap local fruit sits beside a pricey jar of exotic powder
beats.summary: Everyday fruit works as well as rare imported berries, so no powder is needed.

beats.scene: Kofi sneezes into a tissue beside a bowl of oranges and pills
beats.summary: Vitamin C pills do not stop most colds, though they may shorten them slightly.

beats.scene: Amara pins a first star card for fruit and vegetables above the cooker
beats.summary: Fruit and vegetables earn a good rating for groups, and Amara adds them to her Protection Plate.

beats.scene: Kofi tears dark green spinach leaves into a hot pan with garlic
beats.summary: A huge bag of spinach shrinks to a spoonful, and leafy greens are packed with vitamins and fibre.

beats.scene: Amara highlights a line in a report on green leafy vegetables in a library
beats.summary: Large groups who eat leafy greens have a lower risk of heart disease, again a link.

beats.scene: A pill organiser and a bag of kale stand on Mr Danso's kitchen table
beats.summary: Mr Danso takes warfarin, and vitamin K in greens matters to him, so he asks his doctor.

beats.scene: Popeye's cartoon spinach tin is propped beside a bowl of cooked spinach and lemon
beats.summary: Spinach has iron, but plant iron is absorbed less well, and vitamin C helps.

beats.scene: Broccoli, cabbage and cauliflower stacked in a wooden crate at a market stall
beats.summary: Broccoli, cabbage and their relatives contain sulphur compounds, and overcooked cabbage smells of them.

beats.scene: A lab bench with a green extract in a test tube beside a book
beats.summary: Lab results on sulforaphane look exciting, but groups of people show only modest, mixed links.

beats.scene: Amara steams broccoli in a pot with a glass lid until bright green
beats.summary: Gentle cooking keeps more vitamins, while long boiling lets them escape into the water.

beats.scene: Two plates of broccoli, one bright and one grey, sit side by side
beats.summary: Amara compares broccoli steamed for two minutes with boiled for fifteen and admits she cannot measure vitamins at home.

beats.scene: Efua tastes a green stew from a ladle and raises her eyebrows
beats.summary: Kofi hides greens in a stew, and the family eats them without complaint.

beats.scene: Amara sketches a green corner on her Protection Plate beside a warning note
beats.summary: Greens go on the plate, with a note to ask a doctor if you take medicine.

beats.scene: Ripe red tomatoes simmer in olive oil in a shallow pan with basil leaves
beats.summary: Tomatoes contain the red pigment lycopene, which the body absorbs better when they are cooked with a little oil.

beats.scene: A tin of tomatoes sits beside a fresh one and red sauce
beats.summary: Tinned tomatoes are as good as fresh ones, and cooking even adds to the lycopene you can use.

beats.scene: Amara draws a question mark on a page beside a tomato
beats.summary: The research on tomatoes is mixed, and lycopene pills have not been shown to help.

beats.scene: A carrot and an old wartime poster of a night fighter plane
beats.summary: Carrots give vitamin A for eyes, but the wartime night-vision story was a cover for radar.

beats.scene: Kofi chops an onion with watering eyes beside a bulb of garlic
beats.summary: Cutting an onion releases a gas that makes the eyes water, and Kofi shares tricks to stop the tears.

beats.scene: Garlic cloves in a mortar and a big hand-written note saying cures colds
beats.summary: Kofi swears garlic cures colds, but Amara finds only weak evidence.

beats.scene: A pan of onions slowly turning golden beside a bowl of spices
beats.summary: Onions and garlic are part of healthy cooking worldwide, and flavour helps people eat more vegetables.

beats.scene: Red, yellow and green peppers cut open on a board beside an orange
beats.summary: A red pepper holds more vitamin C than an orange, gram for gram.

beats.scene: A salad bowl and a hot stew bowl on one table with laughing family
beats.summary: Some nutrients survive raw and others improve cooked, so eating both works well.

beats.scene: Amara colours in a red slice on the Protection Plate drawing
beats.summary: The plate fills up, and Kofi jokes they need a bigger plate.

beats.scene: Beans, lentils and chickpeas steam in three pots on a crowded stove
beats.summary: Beans, lentils and chickpeas are cheap, tasty, and the star of Kofi's old restaurant menu.

beats.scene: A cook stirs a pot of red kidney beans with a thermometer and timer
beats.summary: Beans are rich in protein, fibre and minerals, but raw kidney beans are poisonous and must be boiled hard.

beats.scene: Amara counts grams of fibre in a notebook beside a food packet
beats.summary: Fibre helps digestion and the heart, health bodies suggest about twenty-five to thirty grams a day, and many people eat less.

beats.scene: A cartoon of tiny microbes cheering inside a drawing of a gut
beats.summary: Fibre feeds trillions of gut microbes, and the research on them is still young.

beats.scene: Zainab holds her stomach and laughs at a bowl of bean stew
beats.summary: Beans can cause wind, which fades if you start small and rinse tinned beans.

beats.scene: A scientist's chart in a library book shows cholesterol dropping after bean meals
beats.summary: Several small trials found that eating beans and lentils lowers cholesterol a little.

beats.scene: A bowl of porridge oats topped with sliced banana and a spoon beside it
beats.summary: Oats contain beta-glucan, which helps lower cholesterol, and plain oats beat sweet instant packets.

beats.scene: Three jars of whole grains stand beside a loaf of dark seeded bread
beats.summary: Whole grains are linked with lower risk of heart disease and diabetes; check the ingredients for real whole grain.

beats.scene: Kofi stirs a big pot of white rice while Amara frowns at it
beats.summary: White rice is not poison, and mixing whole grains with it is an easy start.

beats.scene: A cooking pot of lentil stew feeds six people at a table
beats.summary: One cheap pot feeds six, and Amara adds beans and oats to the Plate with a cost note.

beats.scene: A small handful of mixed nuts in a cupped hand above a wooden table
beats.summary: A small handful of nuts is about thirty grams, and walnuts, almonds and peanuts are good choices unsalted.

beats.scene: Amara reads a study summary in a library about nuts and heart health
beats.summary: Large groups link nuts a few times a week with lower heart disease risk, but nuts are energy rich.

beats.scene: A no-nuts sign hangs on a school door beside an empty lunch box
beats.summary: Nut allergies can be serious, so never share nuts with an allergic person and always read labels.

beats.scene: A toddler's bowl with a spoonful of smooth nut butter and a nurse's chart
beats.summary: Whole nuts can choke small children, and advice about babies and nuts has changed, so parents should ask their doctor.

beats.scene: Pumpkin and sunflower seeds toast in a dry pan on the stove
beats.summary: Seeds are a nut-free choice with similar minerals and healthy fats.

beats.scene: Olive oil pours from a green bottle onto a plate of bread and salad
beats.summary: Olive oil is mostly healthy fat, and a peppery taste shows it is rich in plant substances.

beats.scene: A map of Spain with a researcher holding a clipboard in a clinic
beats.summary: In Spain about seven thousand older adults at risk of heart disease joined a trial of the Mediterranean diet.

beats.scene: A clinic hall with three groups seated at tables with different foods
beats.summary: Those given extra olive oil or nuts had about thirty percent fewer major heart events than the low-fat group.

beats.scene: A page headed corrected study lies beside a tray of olives and bread
beats.summary: The study was republished in 2018 after problems with how some people were assigned, and the result held.

beats.scene: Amara dresses a salad with a measured spoon of olive oil as Kofi watches
beats.summary: Olive oil is rich in energy, so measure it, and swap butter for plant oils.

beats.scene: Amara and Kofi grill a silver fish at an outdoor stove
beats.summary: Oily fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel contain omega-3 fats the body cannot make well.

beats.scene: A bottle of fish oil capsules stands next to a grilled sardine
beats.summary: Fish eaters have lower heart risk in groups, but trials of fish oil capsules in healthy people show little benefit.

beats.scene: A tin of sardines is opened beside bread and tomato slices
beats.summary: Tinned sardines and mackerel are cheap, oily and keep for months.

beats.scene: A chart on a clinic wall shows fish with warning pictures of a shark
beats.summary: Some big fish contain mercury, so pregnant women and small children are told to limit them.

beats.scene: Walnuts and flax seeds stand beside a bottle of algae oil
beats.summary: Plant sources give a form of omega-3, and vegans can ask a dietitian about algae oil.

beats.scene: A boiled egg cut in half sits in an egg cup beside toast
beats.summary: Eggs are cheap protein and vitamins, and for most healthy people moderate eating is fine.

beats.scene: A carton of eggs sits in a fridge beside a thermometer
beats.summary: Eggs must be kept cool and cooked firm for babies, older people and in pregnancy as local rules say.

beats.scene: Two cups of yoghurt side by side with a teaspoon of sugar beside each
beats.summary: Plain yoghurt gives protein and calcium, while sweetened ones can hide many spoons of sugar.

beats.scene: A jar of fermented vegetables stands beside a bowl of fermented maize porridge
beats.summary: Fermented foods contain live microbes, but evidence of benefit is early and thin.

beats.scene: Zainab and Amara eat grilled fish and yoghurt at Kofi's table
beats.summary: Zainab joins a fish supper, and Amara rates fish as good in groups and pills as poor.

beats.scene: Kofi pours dark tea from a steaming teapot into two mugs
beats.summary: Tea comes from one plant and holds polyphenols, while herbal teas are a different thing.

beats.scene: A hot mug beside a thermometer that reads very hot
beats.summary: Regular tea drinkers have slightly lower risk in groups, but very hot drinks are linked with throat cancer.

beats.scene: A school bag with an energy drink can beside a glass of milk
beats.summary: Strong tea at meals can block iron, and health agencies advise against energy drinks for children.

beats.scene: A yellow spice jar of turmeric stands next to a bowl of golden curry
beats.summary: Turmeric looks exciting in the laboratory, because its curcumin affects cells in a dish.

beats.scene: A tiny amount of yellow powder in a test tube with a pepper mill
beats.summary: The body absorbs little curcumin, black pepper helps a bit, and human trials are small and weak.

beats.scene: A bottle of turmeric capsules with a warning leaflet beside a curry bowl
beats.summary: High-dose turmeric pills have rarely been linked to liver problems, while curry in food is fine.

beats.scene: Amara breaks a square of dark chocolate and holds it up to the light
beats.summary: Dark chocolate contains cocoa flavanols, small trials show small effects, but it also contains sugar and fat.

beats.scene: Zainab blindfolded in a classroom tasting two squares of chocolate with cups
beats.summary: Amara and Zainab run a blind chocolate taste test to learn how fair tests work.

beats.scene: A wooden spice box with small jars of ginger, cumin and chilli
beats.summary: Spices add flavour that lets people use less salt and sugar, and flavour keeps people eating well.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro reads Amara's progress notes at her desk with a pencil
beats.summary: Mrs Okoro asks what evidence would change Amara's mind about turmeric, and Amara knows the answer.

beats.scene: Frozen peas and tinned beans are poured into a pot in a busy kitchen
beats.summary: Frozen vegetables are frozen soon after picking, so they keep their vitamins and never go to waste.

beats.scene: Tins of tomatoes, sweetcorn and sardines stacked on a pantry shelf
beats.summary: Tinned food keeps most nutrients, so choose no added salt or sugar and rinse the beans.

beats.scene: A limp week-old lettuce next to a fresh frozen bag of spinach
beats.summary: Fresh vegetables lose vitamins as they sit, so frozen can beat a tired fresh one.

beats.scene: Amara holds a small purse among market stalls beside Auntie Grace
beats.summary: Kofi sets Amara a budget, and Auntie Grace shows how to find the best prices.

beats.scene: A shopping basket holding cabbage, beans, oats and carrots beside a small purse
beats.summary: Beans, oats, cabbage, carrots, eggs, tinned fish and frozen vegetables are cheap and nutritious.

beats.scene: Kofi simmers vegetable peelings and bones in a big pot for stock
beats.summary: Kofi hates waste, and use by and best before dates mean different things.

beats.scene: A farmer's cart of pumpkins and tomatoes in the late afternoon sun
beats.summary: Seasonal produce is cheaper and tastier, and prices fall at the end of the market day.

beats.scene: A kitchen fridge with raw chicken on the bottom shelf and a rice pot
beats.summary: Cold storage matters, and cooked rice must be cooled fast and refrigerated.

beats.scene: A long supermarket queue with a woman counting coins at the front
beats.summary: Advice must fit a person's money, time and culture, and not everyone lives near fresh food.

beats.scene: Amara and Kofi serve a one-pot dinner to six with a cost chart
beats.summary: Their one-pot dinner for six costs little, and Amara adds a cost column to her chart.

beats.scene: Amara carries a full water bottle while her friend holds a fizzy sugary drink
beats.summary: Water is the best everyday drink, and tap water is cheap.

beats.scene: Nine spoons of sugar piled in a glass beside a can of fizzy drink
beats.summary: Amara spoons out the sugar in a can of fizzy drink, and Zainab is shocked.

beats.scene: A child holds a sugar-free drink in a bright classroom of the Netherlands
beats.summary: Too much sugar is linked with tooth decay and weight gain, and a Dutch trial of children backs this up.

beats.scene: A bowl of sugar with a measuring spoon beside a biscuit and a label
beats.summary: The WHO advises free sugars stay under ten percent of energy, about twelve teaspoons, and less is better.

beats.scene: Amara hunts through the cupboard reading labels on ketchup, cereal and sauce
beats.summary: Sugar hides in sauces and cereals under names such as glucose syrup and honey.

beats.scene: A diet drink beside a notice about non-sugar sweeteners with a question mark
beats.summary: The WHO advised in 2023 that sweeteners are not a good way to control weight.

beats.scene: A bowl of whole fruit and a glass of juice stand side by side
beats.summary: Whole fruit keeps its fibre, while juice and smoothies count as free sugars.

beats.scene: A birthday party with children running, a cake and a clock on the wall
beats.summary: Trials found sugar does not make children wild, and the party and expectations do.

beats.scene: Kofi slowly eats a slice of cake at a table with candles
beats.summary: Treats can be enjoyed slowly, and guilt is not a health plan.

beats.scene: Amara counts drinks in her class on a tally sheet while water jugs wait
beats.summary: Amara surveys her class, and a water jug goes on every table.

beats.scene: A salt shaker beside fresh herbs and lemons on a wooden counter
beats.summary: The WHO advises less than five grams of salt a day, about one level teaspoon.

beats.scene: A blood pressure cuff on an arm with a nurse and a chart
beats.summary: Too much salt raises blood pressure, and trials show cutting salt lowers it within weeks.

beats.scene: A pie chart of salt in a sandwich, soup, sauce and bread
beats.summary: Most salt comes from bread, soups, sauces and processed food, not the shaker.

beats.scene: Amara reads a bread label while Kofi holds a stock cube
beats.summary: Bread and stock cubes are saltier than expected, and Kofi is surprised.

beats.scene: A pan of stew with lemon, herbs and chilli on a wooden board
beats.summary: Herbs, spices, lemon and garlic can replace salt, and taste buds adjust within weeks.

beats.scene: A bunch of bananas, spinach and beans on a scale beside a salt jar
beats.summary: Potassium in beans, greens and bananas may blunt the effect of salt.

beats.scene: A doctor writes on a clipboard while an older person listens
beats.summary: Some people need less salt and some need more, so a doctor must say which.

beats.scene: Amara compares two soup tins by the per hundred grams column
beats.summary: Amara learns to compare labels per hundred grams and by colour codes.

beats.scene: Kofi sits alone with a large pot of old restaurant stew looking sorry
beats.summary: Kofi admits his restaurant used a lot of salt to bring people back.

beats.scene: Efua and Zainab taste two stews blindfolded at the kitchen table
beats.summary: A salt-light stew passes a family taste test, and herbs join the plate.

beats.scene: A tray of sausages and ham slices next to a plate of grilled vegetables
beats.summary: Meat gives protein, iron and B12, and the question is which kind and how much.

beats.scene: A group of experts around a long table at a conference in 2015
beats.summary: In 2015 a panel of experts from ten countries reviewed the evidence on meat and cancer.

beats.summary: Ultra-processed foods are made mostly from industrial ingredients you would not find in a kitchen.

beats.scene: A small research ward with twenty adults at a long table
beats.summary: A small 2019 hospital trial found people ate about five hundred more calories a day on an ultra-processed diet.

beats.summary: Not all processed food is bad, and the line is blurry, so look at ingredients.

beats.summary: Alcohol raises the risk of several cancers, including mouth, throat, bowel and breast.

beats.summary: The old claim that red wine is healthy came from studies with flaws.

beats.scene: A teenager with a juice glass at a table while the family toasts
beats.summary: The WHO says no level of alcohol is completely safe, and young people and pregnant women should avoid it.

beats.scene: Kofi lifts blackened toast from a grill and waves away the smoke
beats.summary: Burnt starchy food makes a chemical called acrylamide, so aim for golden, not brown.

beats.summary: Grilling meat hot makes harmful compounds, so cook gently and cut away burnt bits.

beats.summary: Reused frying oil breaks down, so cook with less oil and gentler heat.

beats.scene: A dish of mouldy peanuts and a sealed dry storage tin
beats.summary: Mould on groundnuts and grains can make toxins, so store them dry and throw mouldy ones away.

beats.scene: Four pans labelled steam, boil, bake and stir fry on a stove
beats.summary: Steaming, boiling, baking and stir frying each have trade-offs, and the best method keeps you eating vegetables.

beats.summary: Amara makes a safer kitchen poster for her display.

beats.scene: A bottle of vitamin A capsules with a warning triangle next to carrots

beats.summary: Ms Adebayo says her advice is general and she checks each person before suggesting pills.

beats.scene: A winter street scene with a thin sun and a bottle of vitamin D
beats.summary: Some people run low in vitamin D in winter, and a doctor can test.

beats.scene: A grapefruit beside a medicine box with a warning sticker
beats.summary: Natural does not mean safe, as St John's wort and grapefruit can change how medicines work.

beats.summary: Amara tests an influencer's claim with her questions: who, how many, what kind and who is paid.

beats.scene: Kofi holds an old cigarette lighter above a bin

beats.scene: A teenager sits with a trusted adult at a quiet kitchen table
beats.summary: Food may help mood a little, but it is not a treatment for depression, so talk to a doctor.

B1B2: Amara's teacher, Mrs Okoro, says any topic is fine for the science project if the evidence is honest. Amara picks food, because she wants to know which foods really help the body.
Her grandfather Kofi ran a small restaurant for thirty years, and he offers to help with the project. He says he has fed thousands of people but has never studied what is inside the food.
Amara and Kofi write food sayings on yellow notes and stick them on the fridge. Carrots are good for the eyes, garlic stops colds, and sugar makes children wild.
Kofi opens an old restaurant notebook full of stains and names. His regulars each swore that one special food kept them healthy, and no two of them agreed.
Amara writes “Show the evidence” in large letters at the top of her page. Kofi nods and adds that in a kitchen, a rule must be tasted too.
At school, Mrs Okoro asks Amara what she means by the word protect. Amara has to turn her big idea into a question that a test could answer.
Mrs Okoro writes two columns on the board, one for good sources and one for weak ones. Health agencies and big reviews are good, but “my uncle said” is not.
Amara and Kofi plan the next eight weeks on a paper calendar. First comes the body and the evidence, then the foods, then a plan, and finally the Science Fair.
Amara draws a big empty plate on a piece of card and calls it the Protection Plate. Kofi taps it with his spoon and promises to taste everything that goes on it.
That night Amara cannot sleep, so she writes her first question in her notebook. In the morning she finds a note from Kofi saying to start with the body, not the food.
Kofi shows Amara a long pale scar across the back of his hand from an old kitchen knife. Amara wonders how a cut can close itself without any help.
When skin is cut, tiny cells in the blood called platelets rush to the spot. They stick together and build a net of protein, and the plug dries into a scab.
Skin is the body's first wall against germs, and it is not just a wrapper. Its top layer is replaced about every month, so you are always wearing new skin.
Mrs Okoro draws the immune system on the board with guard cells in coloured pens. Some cells fight germs at once, others remember them, and vaccines train that memory without making you ill.
Red blood cells last only about four months before the body replaces them. Even a broken bone knits itself together again, with a little help from a cast.
A builder needs bricks to build a wall, and the body needs materials from food to repair itself. Protein, vitamin C and many other nutrients all play a part.
Mr Quaye, a neighbour, sells bottles of miracle juice that he says can fix every illness. Amara writes in her notebook that food can support the body but it cannot cure everything.
Kofi tells Amara that some illness is just bad luck, or age, or something in the family. A healthy diet can lower the chances, but it cannot give a guarantee.
When a body lacks a nutrient, the right food can fix the problem. But once there is enough, extra amounts usually give little or no further benefit.
That evening Amara types the first page of her report, with a cup of Kofi's tea beside the screen. She writes that the body is the protector, and food is the helper.
Mrs Okoro draws two groups of people on the board, one that eats many vegetables and one that eats few. Scientists follow such groups for years, but this shows links, not proof.
On hot days people buy more ice cream, and they also get more sunburn. Ice cream does not cause sunburn, because a third thing, the sun, causes both.
Amara tries to write down everything she ate last Tuesday and fails after breakfast. Studies that rely on memory are useful, but they are never perfect.
In a trial, scientists use chance to decide who eats what, then compare the groups. Because chance picks the groups, other habits are spread out evenly between them.
In 1747 a ship's surgeon named James Lind gave six different remedies to twelve sailors with scurvy. Two sailors were given oranges and a lemon, and they recovered fastest.
It is hard to make people eat different foods for years, and nobody can hide fish from the person eating it. So many trials are short and measure signs such as cholesterol.
Scientists often test a substance on cells in a dish, or on mice. It may behave very differently inside a person, so a dish result is only a first clue.
Amara draws a ladder of evidence with five rungs on a large card. From the bottom she writes stories, lab studies, groups of people, trials, and finally reviews of many trials.
A newspaper headline shouts, “Chocolate cures everything,” and Kofi is delighted. Amara checks the story and finds that it is based on a small study of mice.
Kofi lays a long table with many different dishes and no single star dish. The pattern of eating over years matters much more than any one superfood.
On Saturday, Amara and Kofi visit the busy market and stop at Auntie Grace's stall. The stall glows with red, yellow, green and purple, like a box of paints.
Plants cannot run away from danger, so they make many substances to protect themselves from sun, insects and germs. Some of these substances may also help the people who eat them.
Eating the rainbow is a useful idea, but colour is only a clue. Cauliflower, onions, bananas and white beans are pale, and they are good foods too.

The World Health Organization advises at least four hundred grams of fruit and vegetables a day, which is about five portions. A portion is roughly what fits in one hand, and potatoes are not counted.
Large studies of many people link eating more fruit and vegetables with a lower risk of heart disease. This is a link and not proof, but it appears again and again.
Amara boils some red cabbage, and the water turns a deep purple. When she squeezes lemon into a glass of it, the colour changes to bright pink.
Berries are rich in anthocyanins, and large studies link them with healthier hearts and blood pressure. The trials so far are small, so any benefit looks modest.
Next to a jar of expensive berry powder, Auntie Grace's plums, oranges and apples cost far less. Amara finds no good evidence that rare berries beat everyday fruit, so the powder is not needed.
Kofi catches a cold and reaches for a bowl of oranges and a pot of vitamin C pills. Reviews of many trials find that regular vitamin C does not stop most colds, though it may shorten them a little.
Amara pins a card above the cooker and gives fruit and vegetables a good rating for evidence in groups of people. She colours the first section of her Protection Plate.
Kofi tears a huge bag of spinach into a hot pan, and it shrinks to almost nothing. Leafy greens are full of vitamins, minerals and fibre for very few calories.
Amara reads that people who eat more green leafy vegetables tend to have a lower risk of heart disease. As before, this is a link from groups of people, not a proof.
Kofi's neighbour Mr Danso takes a medicine called warfarin, and greens contain a lot of vitamin K. Vitamin K helps blood to clot, so people like him must ask their doctor.
Spinach has iron, but the body absorbs the iron in plants less easily than the iron in meat. Vitamin C helps, so a squeeze of lemon on cooked spinach is a smart idea.
Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale and sprouts all belong to one plant family. They contain sulphur compounds, and that is why overcooked cabbage smells so strong.
In the lab, a substance from broccoli called sulforaphane has exciting effects on cells. In groups of people the links are modest and mixed, so Amara is careful.
Cooking vegetables gently keeps more of the good things inside them. Boiling them for a long time lets some vitamins escape into the water.
Amara steams one batch of broccoli for two minutes and boils another for fifteen. The second batch turns grey and soft, but she cannot measure vitamins in a home kitchen.
Kofi blends spinach into a rich tomato stew, and the whole family eats it happily. Amara's mother, Efua, tastes it and raises her eyebrows, because she cannot find the greens.
Amara draws a green section on her Protection Plate and pins a warning note beside it. The note says that anyone who takes medicine should ask a doctor first.
Ripe tomatoes simmer in olive oil with basil leaves, and they smell wonderful. They contain a red substance called lycopene, which the body takes in better from cooked tomatoes with a little oil.
Kofi says that a tin of tomatoes is as useful as a fresh one, and Amara agrees. The heat of the tinning process even makes the lycopene easier for the body to use.
Some studies link tomato foods with a lower risk of certain diseases, but others find nothing. Pills of pure lycopene have not been shown to help, so Amara marks the evidence as mixed.
Carrots contain a substance the body turns into vitamin A, which the eyes need. But the wartime story that carrots gave pilots night vision was a cover for a secret machine called radar.
When Kofi cuts an onion, a gas escapes from the cut cells and stings his eyes. He chills the onion first and uses a very sharp knife, which helps a little.
Kofi swears that garlic cures colds, so Amara searches for the evidence. She finds only a little, from small studies, which is not enough to say that it works.
Onions and garlic appear in healthy cooking all around the world, but the research on them alone is mixed. Tasty food helps people to eat more vegetables, and that is a real benefit.
Gram for gram, a red pepper contains more vitamin C than an orange does. Amara slices red, yellow and green peppers on a board and tastes them all.
Some nutrients survive best in raw food, while others, like lycopene, improve with cooking. So a salad and a hot stew on the same table is a good plan.
Amara colours a red slice on the Protection Plate for tomatoes and peppers. The plate is filling up fast, and Kofi jokes that they need a bigger one.
Kofi cooks beans, lentils and chickpeas in three pots at once, as he did in his restaurant. These foods are cheap, filling and tasty, and they were his best sellers.
Beans are rich in protein, fibre, iron and other minerals. But raw red kidney beans are poisonous, so they must be boiled hard for at least ten minutes.
Health bodies suggest about twenty-five to thirty grams of fibre a day, and many people eat less. Amara counts the fibre in her own meals and is surprised by how low it is.
Trillions of tiny microbes live in the gut, and they feed on the fibre that we cannot digest. Scientists are learning fast about them, but the research is still young.
Amara's best friend Zainab laughs and warns that beans can make people very windy. The wind fades if you start with small amounts, drink water and rinse tinned beans before using them.
Several small trials found that eating beans and lentils lowers cholesterol a little. Because they are trials, they sit high on her ladder, and she is pleased.
Oats contain a fibre called beta-glucan, which helps to lower cholesterol. Plain oats are better than sweet instant packets, which often hide a lot of sugar.
Whole grains such as brown rice, barley, millet and whole wheat keep all parts of the seed. Large studies link them with a lower risk of heart disease and diabetes.
Kofi stirs a big pot of white rice and asks Amara if he has been poisoning people. She laughs and says no, and suggests mixing in some whole grains.
One big pot of lentil stew feeds six people for very little money. Amara adds beans and oats to her Protection Plate and writes the cost beside them.
A handful of nuts is about thirty grams, which many guides suggest for one day. Walnuts, almonds and peanuts are all fine choices, as long as they are not salted.
Large studies link eating nuts a few times a week with a lower risk of heart disease. Small trials also show that nuts lower cholesterol slightly, which fits the larger picture.
A sign on the school door says no nuts, because a nut allergy can be very serious. People with allergies must read every label and must never be given nuts by mistake.
Whole nuts can make small children choke, so they should only eat nut butters or ground nuts. Advice on when babies should first taste nuts has changed, so parents should ask a doctor.
Kofi toasts pumpkin and sunflower seeds in a dry pan until they smell warm. Seeds contain healthy fats and minerals, and they suit many people who cannot eat nuts.
Olive oil is mostly healthy fat, and good oil also holds many plant substances. When Kofi tastes a good extra virgin oil, it makes his throat tickle with a peppery bite.
In Spain, about seven thousand older adults at high risk of heart disease joined a famous trial. One group ate a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil, and another had extra nuts.
After about five years, the groups with extra olive oil or nuts had fewer heart attacks and strokes. The drop was about thirty percent compared with the low-fat group.
In 2018 the scientists published the study again after finding problems with how some people were assigned. They checked their numbers again in different ways, and the result was similar.
Olive oil is rich in energy, so Amara measures it with a spoon. Health bodies also advise swapping butter and ghee for plant oils such as olive oil.
Oily fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel contain omega-3 fats. The body cannot make much of these fats, so they must come from food.
People who eat fish tend to have a lower risk of heart disease, and many guides suggest fish twice a week. But trials of fish oil capsules in healthy people show little benefit.
A tin of sardines costs little and keeps for a long time in the cupboard. Kofi mashes them on bread with tomato and says it is the best lunch in the world.
Large fish such as shark, swordfish and marlin contain more mercury, which can harm a growing baby's brain. Pregnant women and small children are told to limit them, and to ask a doctor or midwife.
Walnuts, flax seeds and rapeseed oil contain a plant form of omega-3. The body turns only a little into the fish kind, so vegans may ask a dietitian about algae oil.
Eggs are a cheap source of protein, vitamin B12 and other nutrients such as choline. Cholesterol in eggs was once feared, but for most healthy people moderate eating is fine.
Eggs should be kept cool, and hands should be washed after touching raw egg. Babies, older people and pregnant women are often advised to eat eggs cooked firm, though local rules differ.
Plain yoghurt gives protein and calcium, but sweet fruit yoghurts can hide many spoons of sugar. Amara piles teaspoons of sugar beside each cup to match what the label says.
Kimchi, sauerkraut, kefir and fermented maize porridge all contain live microbes. Small studies suggest some benefits, but the evidence is still early and thin.
Zainab joins them for a fish supper and asks whether her sweet yoghurt drink counts. Amara explains that the label matters, and she rates fish as good in groups but poor in pills.
True tea comes from one plant and holds plant substances called polyphenols. Herbal teas, made from flowers or leaves of other plants, are a different thing.
In groups of people, regular tea drinkers have a slightly lower risk of heart disease. However, drinks hotter than about sixty-five degrees are linked with throat cancer, so let tea cool first.
Strong tea drunk with meals can block some iron from plant foods. Health agencies also advise against energy drinks for children, because they contain a lot of caffeine.

Turmeric gives curry its golden colour, and a substance in it called curcumin does exciting things to cells in the laboratory. Amara wonders whether the same thing really happens inside a living person.
The body absorbs very little curcumin, although black pepper helps a bit. Trials in people are few, small and weak, so turmeric sits low on Amara's ladder.
High-dose turmeric pills have rarely been linked to liver problems, while turmeric in food is considered safe. Kofi decides that his golden curry is still a delicious dinner, and a healthy one.
Dark chocolate contains cocoa flavanols, and small trials show small effects on blood pressure. But chocolate also contains sugar and fat, so a square or two is enough.
Amara asks Zainab to taste two chocolates with her eyes covered and guess which one is dark. The test shows why fair trials hide the answer, because people's guesses change when they know.
Ginger, cumin, black pepper and chilli add strong flavour to food. Good flavour lets people use less salt and sugar, and tasty food keeps people eating well.
Halfway through the project, Mrs Okoro reads Amara's notes and asks what evidence would change her mind about turmeric. Amara says a large, fair trial in people would do it.
Frozen vegetables are frozen soon after they are picked, so they keep most of their vitamins. In Kofi's busy kitchen, bags of frozen peas never go to waste.
Tins of tomatoes, sweetcorn, beans and sardines keep most of their nutrients. Choose tins with no added salt or sugar, and rinse the beans before using them.
Fresh vegetables lose some of their vitamins as they sit in a shop or fridge for days. So a frozen vegetable can beat a tired fresh one that is a week old.
Kofi gives Amara a small purse and a challenge to buy healthy food for a week. Auntie Grace shows her how to find the best prices.
Amara's basket holds cabbage, beans, oats and carrots, and there is still money left. Eggs, tinned fish and frozen vegetables are also cheap and nutritious.
Kofi simmers vegetable peelings and bones for stock, because he hates waste. Amara learns that use by dates are about safety, while best before dates are about quality.
When a fruit or vegetable is in season, there is plenty of it, so it costs less. Prices often fall further at the end of the market day.
Cold storage matters, so raw chicken goes on the bottom shelf of the fridge, away from other food. Cooked rice must be cooled quickly and put in the fridge, because germs can grow in it.
In a long supermarket queue, Amara sees a woman counting coins carefully. Not everyone has the money, the time or a shop nearby, so advice must fit real lives.
Amara and Kofi cook a one-pot dinner for six, and the cost chart shows how little it takes. Efua is surprised, and Amara's cost column shows the price of the meal for each person.
Water is the best everyday drink, because it has no sugar and costs almost nothing from the tap. Tea, coffee and milk also count, if they are not loaded with sugar.
Amara reads that a can of fizzy drink often holds about thirty-five grams of sugar. She spoons nine teaspoons into a glass, and Zainab stares in shock.
Too much sugar is linked with tooth decay and weight gain. In a Dutch trial, children who drank a sugary drink each day gained more fat than those given a sugar-free one.
The World Health Organization advises that free sugars should stay under ten percent of daily energy, which is about twelve teaspoons. A lower amount is better still, according to the same guide.
Amara reads labels on ketchup, cereal and sauce and finds sugar in all of them. Sugar can hide under names such as glucose syrup, honey and fruit juice concentrate.

Sugar-free drinks contain sweeteners instead of sugar, so they add no sugar to the diet. In 2023 the World Health Organization advised against using sweeteners to control weight, because the evidence of benefit is weak.
Whole fruit keeps its fibre, which helps you feel full. Juice and smoothies count as free sugars, so a small glass is enough, and dried fruit should be a small handful.
Trials in which neither parents nor children knew who had sugar found that sugar did not change children's behaviour. The excitement of the party and what parents expect are the likely causes.
Treats can be part of a healthy life if they are enjoyed slowly and sometimes. Feeling guilty about a slice of cake is not a health plan.
Amara asks her class what they drink at lunch and counts the answers on a tally sheet. After the results, Mrs Okoro agrees to put a water jug on every table.
The World Health Organization advises less than five grams of salt a day, which is about one level teaspoon. Salt is sodium chloride, and the body needs a little, but many people eat much more.

In many people, a lot of salt raises blood pressure, and high blood pressure raises the risk of stroke and heart disease. Trials show that eating less salt lowers blood pressure, often within a few weeks.
In many countries most salt in the diet comes from bread, soups, sauces and processed foods, not from the shaker. A pie chart shows how it adds up in one ordinary sandwich lunch.
Amara reads a bread label and finds more salt than she expected. Kofi picks up a stock cube, reads the label too, and is shocked by how salty it is.
Herbs, spices, lemon juice, vinegar and garlic can add flavour in place of salt. Many people find that their taste adjusts within a few weeks.
Potassium, found in beans, greens, bananas and potatoes, may help to balance the effect of salt on blood pressure. Amara weighs these foods on a scale beside the salt jar.
A doctor writes on a clipboard while an older patient listens. Some people are told to eat even less salt, and a few need more, so only a doctor can say.
Amara learns to compare two soup tins by looking at the column for every hundred grams. Some countries also add red, amber and green colours to show high, medium and low.
Kofi sits alone with a pot of old restaurant stew and admits that he used far too much salt. He says he cooked to make people come back, not to keep them healthy.
Efua and Zainab taste two stews with their eyes closed, one salty and one with herbs. Efua prefers the herb stew, and it joins the plate.
Meat gives protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12, so Kofi loves his stews. The question is not whether meat is bad, but which kind and how much.
In 2015 a panel of experts from ten countries met to review the evidence on meat and cancer. They were brought together by the cancer agency of the World Health Organization.

The experts placed processed meat in Group One, which means the evidence that it can cause bowel cancer is strong. Tobacco is in the same group, but that does not mean that sausages are as dangerous as cigarettes.
Red meat, such as beef, pork, lamb and goat, was placed one step lower, as a probable cause of bowel cancer. Many health guides suggest keeping red meat to a few modest portions a week.
Kofi flavours a bean stew with just a few slices of sausage instead of a whole plate of them. Swapping some meat for beans, fish or eggs is an easy and cheap change.
Chicken and fish need extra care in the kitchen to keep everyone safe. Washing raw chicken only splashes germs around, so cook it well, use separate boards and wash your hands.

Ultra-processed foods are made mostly from industrial ingredients, such as flavourings, thickeners and modified starch. Researchers in Brazil created a system to sort foods by how much processing they have had.
In a small trial in 2019, twenty adults stayed in a research centre and ate two different diets. On the ultra-processed diet they ate about five hundred more calories a day and gained weight.
Bread, tinned beans, frozen peas, yoghurt and cheese are all processed in some way. The line between good and bad is blurry, so reading the ingredients matters most.
Efua comes home late and tired, and she heats a ready meal for the family. Amara decides that her project will never make anyone feel ashamed of a quick dinner.
At a family dinner, Amara sees a glass of water beside a glass of wine. Alcohol raises the risk of several cancers, including cancers of the mouth, throat, liver, bowel and breast.
Old studies seemed to show that people who drank a little wine lived longer. But the non-drinkers they compared with often included people who had quit because they were ill.
The World Health Organization says that no level of alcohol is completely safe, and less is better. Young people and pregnant women are advised not to drink at all.

When starchy foods like toast, chips and roast potatoes are cooked until dark brown, a chemical called acrylamide forms. Some food agencies advise cooking to a golden yellow and avoiding anything burnt.
Cooking meat over very high heat or flames can create harmful compounds. Cooking more gently, cutting off burnt parts and using a marinade may reduce the risk.
Cooking oil that is used again and again breaks down and can fill the kitchen with smoke. Using less oil, and gentler heat, is usually kinder to the food and to the cook.
Mould that grows on damp groundnuts and grain can make a poison called aflatoxin. Store these foods dry, and throw away any that look mouldy or smell strange.
Steaming, boiling, baking and stir frying all have good and bad points. The best method is the one that keeps you eating vegetables and does not burn the food.
Amara draws a Safer Kitchen poster with pictures of washing hands, keeping food cold and cooking food through. She adds golden toast and a sealed tin of nuts at the bottom.
Amara draws a second ring on her plate for foods to keep small. It holds salt, sugar, processed meat and alcohol, and she labels it “keep small.”
Kofi's cupboard is full of vitamin pills that he bought because of adverts. Amara explains that a pill holds a few substances, while a plate of food holds thousands.
Many large trials gave vitamin and mineral pills to healthy people and watched what happened. Mostly they found no clear benefit for heart disease or cancer.
In the 1990s, trials in Finland and the United States gave beta-carotene pills to people who smoked. To everyone's surprise there was more lung cancer in the groups taking the pills.
Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and can build up in the body. Taking very large doses of vitamin A is harmful, especially during pregnancy.
Amara interviews Ms Adebayo, a registered dietitian at the local clinic. A registered dietitian has trained for years and is regulated, while in many places anyone can call themselves a nutritionist.
Ms Adebayo says that most healthy people who eat a varied diet do not need vitamin pills. She adds that her advice is general, and that she always checks the person before she suggests anything.
The skin makes vitamin D when sunlight touches it, so some people run low in winter. People who spend little time outdoors or live far from the equator can ask a doctor for a test.
Some natural foods and herbs can change the way a medicine works in the body. Grapefruit affects some medicines, and the herb St John's wort can weaken others, including some contraceptive pills.
A tub of immune booster powder promises to make the body stronger. But a healthy immune system is balanced, not a muscle that grows bigger, so the claim makes little sense.
Dev, a classmate with a project on supplements, argues with Amara in a friendly way. They disagree about pills but agree that both of them must keep asking questions.
A bag of crisps carries a golden superfood banner. Amara learns that superfood has no scientific meaning, and that it is a word chosen to help the product sell.
A bottle of detox tea promises to wash poisons from the body. The liver and kidneys already do that job every day, and some detox products, such as strong laxatives, can cause harm.
Low-fat foods often have extra sugar added to make up for the taste. A label that says no added sugar can still hide natural sugars, so Amara compares them carefully.
Natural, organic and gluten free are words on packets, and none of them means healthier by itself. Gluten free is vital for people with coeliac disease, but it is not a better diet for everyone.
Ingredients on a label are listed in order of weight, with the biggest first. The maker also chooses the portion size, and it is often smaller than what people really eat.
Amara compares two cereals on the per hundred grams column and finds that one has far more sugar and less fibre. Kofi squints at the small print through his reading glasses.
In some places a claim like “helps lower cholesterol” may only appear on a pack if experts have approved the evidence. The oat claim is one of the few that passed.
Amara watches a glossy wellness video that promises a miracle food, and she tests it with her questions. Who says it, how many people, what kind of study, and who is paid?
One headline says eggs are bad, and the next year another says they are good. The basic advice has hardly changed, and most of the swings come from headlines, not from science.
Mrs Okoro tells Amara that her project has become a way to decide what to believe. Amara builds a poster called Five Questions About Any Food Claim.

The World Health Organization suggests at least an hour a day for teenagers and at least two and a half hours a week for adults. Kofi's knees complain about jogging, so he walks fast beside her instead.
Regular activity is one of the best-supported habits for health, in both groups of people and trials. Any movement counts, from football to dancing to a walk to the market.
Teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep each night. Small trials suggest that tired people feel hungrier, and they often want sugary and fatty foods.
Kofi holds an old cigarette lighter above a bin and tells Amara that he stopped smoking twenty years ago. Not smoking is the biggest single step a person can take for health.
Small trials suggest that a better diet may lift mood a little, but the evidence is still early. Food is not a treatment for depression, and anyone who feels low for long should talk to a doctor.
Studies link shared family meals with healthier eating in children, although families who eat together may differ in other ways. Either way, a meal with friends is slower and more enjoyable.
Kofi cooks his mother's recipe beneath her framed portrait, and the kitchen smells of his childhood. Favourite dishes can be adapted with more vegetables and less salt, without being abandoned.
Amara realises that a project about food could make someone worry too much about every bite. If worry about food takes over, a person should talk to a trusted adult or a doctor.
Eating slowly gives the body time to feel full, and it makes meals more enjoyable. Amara and Kofi put their forks down between bites and try it.
Amara spends a Sunday with a walk, a family lunch and an early night. She writes that health is a pattern of days, not one perfect plate.
Amara's brother Kojo, who is two, pushes away a spoonful of green beans. Efua sighs, because he has refused them for the sixth night in a row.
Children often need to try a new food ten times or more before they accept it. Pressure and bribes usually make it worse, while patience and a good example work better.
Older adults often eat less, but they still need enough protein and nutrients. They should ask a doctor about vitamin D and vitamin B12.
When Amara cooks at home from simple ingredients, she controls how much salt, sugar and fat go into the pot. Her mother reads the recipe aloud, and they work as a team.
Amara makes orange lentil soup by frying onions, adding carrots and lentils, and simmering everything with water. Kofi tells her to taste as she goes and to add the lemon at the end.
The final Protection Plate is half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein. It also has plant oil, water and a small corner labelled “keep small.”
Amara and her family try the Protection Plate for seven days, and she writes down what happens. She knows that one family is not a trial, so she is careful about what she claims.
On the fourth day the fridge is almost empty and Efua is exhausted. A bag of frozen peas, some eggs and rice rescue dinner, and Amara learns that plans need to bend.
At the end of the week, the family looks at the chart of ticks and notes. The results show cost, taste and how easy it was, but not any change in health.
Amara and Kofi proofread her report with pencils and cups of tea. She ends it with a list called What We Do Not Know, because honest science admits its gaps.
On the morning of the Fair, Amara sets up her display board in the bright school hall. Kofi arrives early in his best shirt, carrying a basket of real food for the table.
Dev and Zainab have boards next to hers, and visitors wander past all three. Amara explains the ladder of evidence to a small child, who understands it at once.

A parent leans in and asks Amara what people should actually eat. Amara answers that the pattern matters most, with plenty of plants, beans, whole grains and fish, less salt and sugar, and real enjoyment.
A visitor holds up a bottle of a miracle product and asks if it works. Amara points to her poster, asks the five questions, and says that “I don't know” is a good answer.
Dr Mensah, a visiting nutrition researcher, asks whether these foods prevent disease. Amara answers honestly that they may lower the risk, but that no food can guarantee anything.
Dr Mensah asks what Amara would do differently, and she points to the limits section on her board. She says she would run a bigger, fairer test and ask more experts.
While they wait for the results, Kofi and Amara eat sandwiches on a bench in the corridor. Kofi says that he has learned more in eight weeks than in thirty years of cooking.
Mrs Okoro announces that the Honest Science Prize goes to Amara. Kofi and Amara hold a small trophy on the school steps as the sun sets.
Kofi writes a title on a new notebook page and asks to join Amara's next project. They plan a family cookbook of favourite dishes, made lighter with a little of what they know.

That evening, Amara and Kofi eat a simple supper of beans and rice on the doorstep. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor or a registered dietitian about your own health.
C1C2: Amara stared at the project sheet on the kitchen table, where Mrs Okoro had written that any topic would do as long as the evidence was honest. Food seemed the perfect choice, since everybody eats it and everybody seems to have an opinion about it. She wanted to find out which foods truly help the body look after itself, and which claims were only noise.

Kofi, who had run a small restaurant for thirty years, put down his wooden spoon the moment he heard about the project and offered his help. He admitted that he had fed thousands of people without ever studying what their dinners were doing inside them. It was never too late to learn, he declared, and he went off to find a notebook.

Before long the fridge door was covered in yellow notes, each one carrying a saying that Amara or Kofi had heard since childhood. Carrots were said to sharpen the eyes, garlic to see off colds, and sugar to send children bouncing off the walls. Kofi pointed out that nobody had ever asked how anyone knew any of this, and Amara wrote that question at the top.

Kofi's old restaurant notebook was spotted with sauce and crowded with the names of his regulars. One old man swore by fish on Fridays, a nurse by dark chocolate, and a taxi driver by a raw garlic clove every morning. They were all healthy, all certain, and all different, which only made Amara more curious.

Across the top of a clean page, Amara wrote the one rule that the whole project would follow, which was “Show the evidence.” Kofi read it over her shoulder, nodded slowly, and added that in his kitchen a rule was worthless until somebody had tasted it. They shook hands on it, and agreed to follow both rules faithfully for the whole of the next eight weeks.

Mrs Okoro listened to Amara's idea and then asked the question that every good scientist has to answer, which was exactly what she meant by protect. After some thought, Amara wrote that she wanted to learn which everyday foods may help the body look after itself, and how sure anyone can be. The word may, her teacher said with a smile, was the beginning of honest science.

On the whiteboard, Mrs Okoro drew two columns and told the class where honest evidence comes from. Health agencies, universities and careful reviews of many studies belonged on the left, while a friend's cousin who had once read something online belonged on the right. Amara copied both columns into her notebook and underlined the word reviews twice, because that, she suspected, was where the real answers would be found.

Kofi found an old paper calendar and the two of them stuck it to the fridge beside the yellow notes. The first week would cover the body and the nature of evidence, the middle weeks would test the foods one by one, and the last would be given to a plan and the Science Fair. Kofi circled the day of the Fair in thick pencil and said that cooks always work to a deadline.

On a large piece of card, Amara drew a plain round plate and gave it a name, the Protection Plate. By the end of the eight weeks she hoped to fill it with everyday foods that had earned their place through honest evidence. Kofi tapped the empty circle with his wooden spoon and solemnly promised to taste every single thing that went onto it.

That night, Amara lay awake with the notebook open on her blanket and wrote the first real question of the project, which was what the body is already doing to protect itself. In the morning she found a note from Kofi on the kitchen table, propped against the sugar bowl. It said, in his big careful handwriting, that a good cook learns the kitchen before the recipe, so they would start with the body and not the food.

Kofi held his hand under the kitchen light and showed Amara a long pale scar, a souvenir of a very sharp knife and a very busy Friday night. Over thirty years of cooking he had collected a small gallery of such marks, each one a story. Amara realised she had never really asked how a cut manages to close itself.

Within seconds of a cut, tiny blood cells called platelets rush to the damaged spot and clump together like sandbags against a flood. They weave a net of a protein called fibrin, and the net traps more cells until a firm clot has formed. Beneath the dark scab that follows, the body is already quietly building new skin.

Amara pressed her fingers against her forearm and Kofi explained that skin is far more than a wrapper, because it is the first wall against germs and the weather. Its outer layer is shed and replaced about every month, which means that she is never wearing quite the same skin for long. It was strange, she thought, to be a machine that rebuilds its own surface as it goes.

Mrs Okoro filled the whiteboard with coloured pens, drawing a first wall of skin, a patrol of cells that attack germs at once, and a slower force that remembers each invader for years. Vaccines, she explained, train that memory safely, which is why no food, however healthy, can ever replace them. Amara copied the diagram and wrote beneath it that food helps the immune system do its job but never does it for the body.

Amara learned that her body is constantly renewing itself, because red blood cells wear out after about four months and are replaced by fresh ones. Even a broken bone repairs itself, knitting together over weeks while a doctor's cast keeps it steady. Behind every healed cut and mended bone is a crew of cells that never stops working.

Kofi compared the body to a building site, where the skilled workers are already on the job but cannot work without bricks, timber and tools. Food delivers those materials, such as protein for repairs, vitamin C to help build the stretchy protein in skin, and a long list of minerals and other nutrients. A body short of materials struggles, but a body with plenty does not become unbreakable.

Down the road, Mr Quaye sold bottles of a bright green miracle juice and promised that it could fix almost any illness. Amara, who now had a rule, asked him for the evidence, and he could offer only a few happy customers. She wrote in her notebook that food can support the body's own protection, but that anyone who promises a cure is selling something.

Kofi sat on the porch step and told Amara that one of his friends had eaten well all his life and still fallen ill. Some illnesses come from age, from genes or from plain bad luck, and nobody deserves the blame for them. Food can tilt the odds a little, he said, but it can never give a guarantee, and a good scientist must be kind about that.

Amara found that the rule of enough runs through all of nutrition, because a body short of iron or vitamin C really does need those foods. Once the body has enough, however, a double helping does not make it twice as healthy. More is not always better, she wrote, and sometimes more is simply more expensive.

That evening Amara opened her laptop, set a cup of Kofi's tea beside the screen, and typed the first page of her report. She wrote that the body is the protector, with its skin, its immune system and its endless cell repair, and that food is only the helper. Kofi, reading over her shoulder, said it was the best sentence in the whole project so far.

On the whiteboard, Mrs Okoro drew two groups of people, one that eats plenty of vegetables and one that eats hardly any. Scientists follow groups like these for many years and watch who stays well, which reveals useful links between food and health. A link, she warned the class, is a clue worth following, but it is never a proof.

Mrs Okoro gave the class a famous puzzle, which is that ice cream sales and sunburn rise and fall together through the year. Nobody believes that ice cream burns the skin, because the real cause of both is the summer sun. The same trap hides in food studies, since people who eat many vegetables often also exercise, avoid smoking and have more money.

Mrs Okoro set a small test, asking everyone to write down every single thing they had eaten last Tuesday. Amara remembered breakfast, half of lunch and a vague biscuit, and the whole class discovered how unreliable memory can be. Large studies often depend on exactly this kind of recollection, so their results must be read with care.

A trial works differently, because the scientists use chance, like a coin toss, to decide who eats which food. Since chance does the choosing, the exercisers, the smokers and the rich and poor are spread evenly between the groups, so any difference can be blamed on the food. Kofi said it was like tasting two soups side by side, with the cook out of the room.

In 1747, aboard a British warship, a surgeon named James Lind took twelve sailors suffering from scurvy and gave each pair a different remedy, including cider, vinegar and seawater. The two men given oranges and a lemon recovered fastest, long before anyone knew that vitamin C existed. It was one of the first fair comparisons in the history of medicine, and it was about food.

Food trials are difficult in ways that drug trials are not, because nobody can swallow a hidden fish, and few people will follow a strict diet for ten years. Many trials therefore last only weeks and measure signs such as cholesterol or blood pressure instead of illness itself. In the end, good evidence about food comes from putting several imperfect kinds of study together and seeing what they agree on.

Many exciting headlines begin in a laboratory, where a substance is dripped onto cells in a dish or fed to mice. Amara noted that soap also kills germs in a dish, but nobody would recommend drinking it, so a dish result is only a first clue. The step from a petri dish to a human being is long, and most ideas fall on the way.

On a large piece of card, Amara drew a ladder with five rungs, and Kofi pinned it to the wall beside the stove. From the bottom upwards she wrote stories, lab studies, groups of people watched over time, trials, and finally reviews that combine many trials together. Every food in the project, she decided, would be placed on the ladder before it earned a place on the Plate.

A headline in the newspaper shouted that chocolate cures everything, and Kofi, who loved chocolate, was delighted. Amara fetched the magnifying glass and looked behind the headline, only to find a small study on mice paid for by a chocolate company. She taught Kofi to ask who did the study, how many were in it, what kind it was and how big the effect had been.

At the end of the week, Kofi laid the long family table with beans, greens, fish, rice, fruit and a little of everything, and not one dish played the starring role. That, he said, was the lesson of the whole week, because the pattern of eating over many years matters far more than any single superfood. Amara pinned a second rule beside the first, which read, “Look at the whole table.”

On Saturday morning, Amara and Kofi walked through the noisy market to the stall of Auntie Grace, who had sold fruit and vegetables there for twenty years. Her tables glowed with red, orange, green and purple, like a giant box of paints. Plants, Kofi said, contain thousands of natural substances, and many of them give the colours that Amara could see.

A plant cannot run away from a hungry insect or hide from the midday sun, so it protects itself with chemistry instead. Many of those substances give fruit and vegetables their colours, their bitterness and their smells, and some of them may also help the people who eat them. Amara wrote that word may again, because hopeful guesses are not the same as results.

Eating the rainbow is a cheerful slogan, and it encourages variety, but Amara noticed that colour is a clue rather than a rule. Cauliflower, onions, bananas and white beans are all pale, and each of them has a place on a healthy table. The real aim is variety, so that no single plant has to do all the work.

The World Health Organization advises eating at least four hundred grams of fruit and vegetables every day, which comes to about five portions of eighty grams each.
