Amara weighed a pile of vegetables on the kitchen scale and was surprised by how large the heap looked. In the official count, potatoes and other starchy roots do not count, because they play a different role on the plate.

Amara read a thick report which showed that, across many countries and many large studies, people who eat more fruit and vegetables have a lower risk of heart disease. She reminded herself that this is a link and not a proof, since vegetable lovers may also differ in other ways. Still, a link that appears again and again, in different places, is worth taking seriously.

In the kitchen, Amara boiled half a red cabbage until the water turned a deep, inky purple, and then poured some into a glass. When she squeezed lemon into it the liquid flashed bright pink, and a pinch of baking soda turned it green. The colour came from a family of plant substances called anthocyanins, which are also what makes berries blue and red.

Amara washed blueberries and strawberries in a white bowl while she read about them, because berries are rich in anthocyanins. Large studies link regular berry eating with healthier hearts and slightly lower blood pressure, and some small trials point the same way. The effect, however, is modest, and it would be wrong to treat a punnet of berries as armour.

On a shelf at a nearby shop, a jar of exotic berry powder cost more than a week of Auntie Grace's plums, oranges and apples. Amara searched for good evidence that rare berries beat everyday fruit and could not find any. Whatever grows near you, she concluded, is the sensible choice, and the powder was a poor use of money.

When Kofi caught a cold, he piled oranges on the table and swore that the vitamin C would send the illness packing. Amara had looked it up, and large reviews of many trials show that regular vitamin C does not prevent colds in most people, although it may shorten them slightly. Kofi ate the oranges anyway, because they were delicious, and he said that was reason enough.

Amara pinned a new card above the cooker and rated fruit and vegetables on her evidence ladder, giving them a high place for large studies of groups and a lower place for trials. Then she took a pencil and coloured in the first, generous section of her Protection Plate. It was a modest beginning, but it was a beginning that she could defend.

Kofi tore dark green spinach leaves into a hot pan with garlic, and the enormous bag collapsed into a single modest spoonful. Leafy greens such as spinach, kale and collards are packed with vitamins, minerals and fibre, yet they carry very few calories. Amara laughed that it was the most impressive disappearing trick she had ever seen in a kitchen.

In the library, Amara highlighted a line in a long report which said that people who eat more green leafy vegetables tend to have a lower risk of heart disease. The studies followed large groups for many years, so they were strong in size but, like all such studies, unable to prove cause. She placed greens on the middle of her evidence ladder and added a small note about the limits.

Mr Danso, who lived next door, took a blood-thinning medicine called warfarin, and he explained to Amara that the vitamin K in leafy greens affects how it works. His doctor had told him not to avoid greens but to keep the amount steady from week to week. Amara pinned a bold note to her plan saying that anyone on medicine should ask a doctor or pharmacist before changing what they eat.

Kofi had always believed that spinach made people strong, in the manner of the old cartoon sailor, so Amara checked what it really contains. Spinach does contain iron, but the body absorbs plant iron less easily than the iron in meat, and vitamin C helps to improve the difference. A squeeze of lemon over cooked spinach, she told him, is therefore both delicious and sensible.

At Auntie Grace's stall the broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale and sprouts sat together in a wooden crate, because they all belong to one great family of plants. Their sharp smell comes from sulphur compounds, which is why overcooked cabbage can fill a whole house with an unwelcome aroma. Kofi groaned and said that he could still smell the school dinners of his childhood.

Laboratory studies of a substance from broccoli called sulforaphane caused a great deal of excitement, since it seemed to wake up the cell's own defences. When Amara turned to studies of people, however, the links with lower risk of some diseases were modest and mixed. By now she recognised the pattern, in which lab results climb high on the ladder of headlines and low on the ladder of proof.

Amara steamed her broccoli in a pot with a glass lid, and watched it turn from dull green to a bright, glossy colour in a few minutes. Gentle cooking keeps more of the good things in vegetables, whereas long boiling lets vitamins such as vitamin C and folate leak into the water. Kofi, ever thrifty, reminded her that the cooking water makes a fine base for soup.

Amara steamed one batch of broccoli for two minutes and boiled another for a full fifteen, and the difference in colour, smell and texture was plain to see. The long-boiled batch had turned grey and soft, but she admitted in her notebook that a home kitchen has no way to measure vitamins. For that, she wrote, she would have to trust food laboratories and their published work.

For people who dislike greens, Kofi had a trick that he had used in the restaurant for years, which was to chop spinach finely and stir it into a thick, spicy tomato stew. Amara's mother, Efua, tasted a spoonful, raised her eyebrows, and could not find the greens anywhere in the pot. There is no shame in a trick that gets more vegetables onto more plates, Kofi said, so long as the cook is honest about it afterwards.

Amara coloured a green section onto her Protection Plate, and beside it she pinned the warning note about medicines and vitamin K. Greens had earned their place through consistent links in large studies, but the note reminded everyone that no list of foods can know a person's health. Kofi read both and said that the best cooks and the best scientists are the ones who admit what they do not know.

Ripe red tomatoes simmered in a shallow pan of olive oil with torn basil leaves, and the whole kitchen smelled of summer. Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, the red pigment that gives them their colour, and the body absorbs it far better from cooked tomatoes eaten with a little fat. Kofi, who had cooked tomato sauce for thirty years, announced that his habits had been scientific all along.

Kofi pulled a tin of tomatoes from the cupboard and declared that it was as useful as any fresh tomato, and often cheaper and riper. Amara confirmed that the heat used in the tinning process actually makes the lycopene easier for the body to take up. She added a note that tins should be chosen without added salt or sugar, and that a quick look at the label is always worthwhile.

Amara drew a question mark beside the tomato on her chart, because the research was less tidy than the colour. Some studies of groups link tomato foods with a lower risk of certain diseases, while others find nothing at all, and trials of lycopene pills have not shown clear benefits. Tomatoes were certainly a good food to eat, she decided, but she could not promise that they were protectors.

Carrots contain beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A, a nutrient the eyes truly need in dim light. The famous wartime story that carrots gave pilots night vision, however, was spread in Britain to hide a secret new invention called radar. Eating extra carrots will not give anyone superhuman sight, Kofi concluded, but a person who is short of vitamin A really does struggle in the dark.

Kofi chopped an onion beside a bulb of garlic, and soon tears were running down his cheeks, because cutting the onion releases a gas that irritates the eyes. A sharp knife, a chilled onion and a bit of patience all help to reduce the damage, he said, wiping his face on his apron. In thirty years of cooking he had never found a way to stop the tears completely.

Kofi crushed a clove of garlic in a mortar and swore that it had cured every cold he had ever had. Amara searched for evidence and found only a few small studies, which made a careful review conclude that there was not enough proof to say either way. The only certain effect, she wrote, is that garlic makes the dinner taste wonderful and the cook smell rather strong.

Onions and garlic sit at the start of countless healthy dishes in every part of the world, from lentil stews to vegetable soups. Studies of them alone give mixed results, so Amara refused to claim any special power for either one. Their true gift, she realised, is flavour, because food that tastes good persuades people to eat more vegetables.

Amara cut open red, yellow and green peppers on a wooden board and learned that, gram for gram, a red pepper holds more vitamin C than an orange. Green peppers are simply picked earlier, which explains why they taste less sweet and hold fewer of some nutrients. She tasted a slice of each and decided that the red one was the winner in more ways than one.

Kofi laid a crisp salad and a steaming stew side by side, and the family argued happily over which they preferred. Some nutrients, such as vitamin C, survive best in raw food, while others, like lycopene, become easier to use when vegetables are cooked. The sensible answer, Amara announced, was both, and the argument ended with everybody taking seconds.

Amara coloured a red slice onto the Protection Plate for tomatoes and peppers, and she wrote a small label that said mixed evidence but good food. The card was becoming crowded with colours and notes, and Kofi laughed that they would soon need a plate the size of a table. Three weeks of the project were gone, and she felt, for the first time, that she really understood what she was doing.

Kofi crowded three pots onto the stove and set beans, lentils and chickpeas simmering, just as he had done every morning in his restaurant. These humble foods, which scientists call pulses, are cheap, filling and endlessly adaptable, and a good bean stew had always been his best seller. Amara asked him whether he had ever known they were also good for the body.

Beans are rich in protein, fibre, iron, folate and potassium, and they release their energy slowly, which keeps people feeling full for longer. Kofi added a safety lesson from his restaurant days, which was that raw red kidney beans contain a natural poison and must be boiled hard for at least ten minutes. Soaking, rinsing and proper boiling make them perfectly safe, and tinned beans are already cooked.

Fibre is the part of plants that the body cannot digest, and it helps digestion, heart health and the feeling of fullness. Health bodies suggest about twenty-five to thirty grams a day, yet many people in many countries eat much less. Amara counted the fibre in her own meals for one day, using the labels, and discovered that she fell well short.

Inside every gut live trillions of microbes, and the fibre that the body cannot digest is their favourite food. They turn it into substances that may help to keep the gut lining healthy, though scientists admit that their understanding of this tiny world is still young. Amara drew the gut microbes as a cheering crowd at a football match and wrote underneath, probably helpful, not fully understood.

Amara's best friend Zainab came to supper, took one look at the bean stew and announced that beans give people wind. She was right, because gut microbes ferment some of the sugars in beans and release gas as they do. Starting with small portions, rinsing tinned beans and drinking plenty of water usually help the body to adjust over a few weeks.

In a library book of reviews, Amara found that several small trials, in which people ate beans or lentils for a few weeks, showed a slight fall in their cholesterol. Because these were trials rather than mere links, the evidence sat higher on her ladder, and she marked it with a satisfied tick. The effect was modest, the authors cautioned, but it fitted neatly with the larger picture of healthier hearts among people who eat pulses.

Kofi stirred a pot of porridge and topped it with sliced banana, while Amara read that oats contain a sticky fibre called beta-glucan. Health regulators in several places accept that it helps to lower cholesterol, which is one of the few food claims that has been approved after careful review. Plain oats, she noted, are the better choice, since the instant packets with sweet flavours often carry a lot of added sugar.

A whole grain keeps every part of the seed, including the fibre-rich outer bran and the nutritious germ, whereas refined grains lose both in the mill. Large studies link whole grains with a lower risk of heart disease and type two diabetes, and Amara added that these links hold up reasonably well. She warned, however, that a loaf labelled wholegrain may contain very little, so the first ingredient on the label is the one to check.

Kofi frowned at the big pot of white rice he was stirring and asked whether he had been poisoning people for thirty years. Amara laughed and told him that white rice is a perfectly good food, but that swapping some of it for brown rice, barley or whole wheat is an easy step towards more fibre. Healthy eating, she added, is made of small changes that people can actually keep.

One large pot of lentil stew fed six hungry people that evening, and the whole meal cost less than a single takeaway. Amara added beans, lentils and oats to the Protection Plate, and she began a new column on her chart for price, because the best advice in the world is useless if nobody can afford it. Kofi, scraping the pot, said that cheapness had never once spoiled a good stew.

Kofi cupped a small handful of mixed nuts in his palm and told Amara that this, roughly thirty grams, was the daily amount suggested by many guides. Walnuts, almonds, cashews and peanuts, which are really a kind of bean, all count, and the best kinds are plain and unsalted. Nuts are rich in energy for their size, so a handful, he said firmly, does not mean a bag.

At the library, Amara read a summary of large studies which linked eating nuts several times a week with a lower risk of heart disease. Small trials also showed that nuts lower cholesterol slightly, so the two kinds of evidence pointed the same way, which always strengthens a case. She cautioned herself that nut eaters may also live healthier lives in other ways, and the nuts may not deserve all the credit.

On the door of Amara's school hung a sign that read no nuts, because a few pupils in the building had allergies that could be dangerous. For these people even a trace of nut can cause a severe reaction, so they read every label, carry the medicines their doctors prescribe, and rely on everyone else to be careful. Amara added a bold line to her project, which said that nobody should ever give nuts to a person who is allergic.

Efua reminded Amara that whole nuts are a choking danger for children under five, who should have them only as smooth butter or finely ground. The advice about when babies should first taste nuts has also changed over the years, as new research has appeared, so parents are told to ask a doctor or nurse instead of guessing. Science, Amara thought, keeps correcting itself, and that is exactly why it deserves trust.

Kofi toasted pumpkin and sunflower seeds in a dry pan until they smelled warm and nutty, and then scattered them over a salad. Seeds hold healthy fats, minerals and fibre, and they suit many people who cannot eat nuts, although a few people are allergic to sesame and other seeds. Allergies, Amara noted for the second time, make the label the most important thing in the kitchen.

Olive oil poured in a golden stream from a green bottle onto a plate of bread and salad, and Kofi tasted it with great ceremony. Most of its fat is the healthier kind, and fresh extra virgin oil also holds plant substances that give it a peppery bite at the back of the throat. That bite, he told Amara, is the flavour of the real thing, and it is a good sign.

In Spain, researchers recruited about seven thousand older adults who were at high risk of heart disease and divided them by chance into three groups. Two groups were taught a Mediterranean diet, one with free extra virgin olive oil and the other with free nuts, while the third was told to eat less fat. It was a big trial that lasted about five years, and it was exactly the kind of evidence Amara had been looking for.

After about five years, the people who had eaten the Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil or nuts had suffered about thirty percent fewer major heart problems, such as heart attacks and strokes. The result was a high rung on the ladder, because chance had decided who ate what. Amara wrote that this trial was not about one magic food but about a whole pattern of eating, with olive oil and nuts as the most visible parts.

Amara noticed a surprising note in the library book, which said that the first report had been withdrawn and published again in 2018. The scientists had found that some people had not been assigned to their groups by chance as intended, so they repeated the analysis with that in mind and found a similar result. Honest science, she decided, does not hide its mistakes but corrects them in the open.

Amara measured one spoonful of olive oil onto the salad, because even a healthy oil carries a lot of energy in a small amount. Health bodies advise swapping some of the butter and ghee that people cook with for plant oils such as olive or rapeseed oil. She added the whole Mediterranean pattern to her plate, and she graded it as strong evidence for a way of eating rather than for any one ingredient.

Amara and Kofi grilled a silver fish over an outdoor stove, and the smoke smelled like a seaside holiday. Oily fish such as salmon, sardines, mackerel and herring are rich in omega-3 fats, which the body cannot make in large amounts and mostly has to take from food. Kofi said that his customers had always called fish brain food, and Amara promised to check.

Studies of large groups link eating fish with a lower risk of heart disease, and many guides suggest two portions a week, one of them oily. Amara found, however, that big trials of fish oil capsules in healthy people have mostly shown little or no clear benefit. It seemed that the fish on the plate and the oil in the bottle were not the same thing, and that the whole food may matter more than one ingredient.

Kofi opened a tin of sardines and mashed them onto thick bread with slices of tomato, declaring that no restaurant lunch could beat it. Tinned oily fish such as sardines and mackerel cost little, last for months in the cupboard, and the soft bones in them add calcium. Amara decided that the cheapest route to fish twice a week was probably a tin opener.

On a poster in the clinic waiting room, Amara read that large, long-lived fish such as shark, swordfish and marlin collect more mercury, a metal that can harm the developing brain of a baby. Pregnant women and young children are therefore advised to avoid or limit these fish, and to ask a doctor or midwife about the rest. For most other people, the benefits of eating fish are generally thought to outweigh the small risks.

Walnuts, flax seeds and rapeseed oil contain a plant form of omega-3, but the body turns only a small share of it into the forms found in fish. People who eat no fish at all, such as vegans, can ask a dietitian whether a supplement made from algae would suit them. Amara noted that this was a question for a professional who knows the person, and not something a school project could answer.

Kofi sliced a boiled egg in half and propped it in an egg cup beside buttered toast, as he had done on a thousand breakfast menus. Eggs are a cheap source of protein, vitamin B12 and choline, and the cholesterol they contain was once feared, though it now seems to matter much less for most healthy people. Anyone told by a doctor to watch their cholesterol, Amara added, should follow that advice instead of her notes.

Amara placed the eggs in the fridge door beside a small thermometer and reminded everyone that raw egg can carry germs such as salmonella. Hands should be washed after touching it, eggs should be cooked until firm for babies, older people and anyone who is pregnant, and local safety rules should be followed. A good food, she noted, is only truly good if it is stored, handled and cooked with proper care.

Amara set two cups of yoghurt side by side and piled teaspoons of sugar beside each one to match what the labels said. The plain yoghurt, which offers protein and calcium, had almost none, while the sweet fruit yoghurt held enough sugar to fill several teaspoons. A spoon of fresh fruit stirred into plain yoghurt, she concluded, gives the same pleasure with much less sugar.

Kofi opened a jar of fermented vegetables and set it beside a bowl of the sour maize porridge that his mother used to make. Such foods, along with kimchi, sauerkraut and kefir, contain live microbes that have been part of human cooking for thousands of years. Small studies suggest possible benefits for the gut, but Amara wrote honestly that the evidence is early and she could not call it proof.

Zainab joined them for the fish supper and asked, between mouthfuls, whether her sweet yoghurt drink counted as a healthy food. Amara explained that the label would tell her, and that sugar can turn a healthy food into a dessert, while Kofi refilled her plate. That night Amara updated the ladder, giving fish a good place for the whole food and a poor one for the capsules.

Kofi poured dark, steaming tea from a battered pot into two mugs, and explained that real tea, whether black or green, comes from the leaves of a single plant. It is rich in polyphenols, a large family of plant substances, whereas herbal teas are made from other plants and have their own, mostly unstudied, qualities. Amara drank hers slowly and said that tea was the most relaxing thing she had learned about so far.

Studies of large groups link regular tea drinking with a slightly lower risk of heart disease, though tea drinkers may differ in other ways, and a spoonful of sugar would cancel some of the good. A separate finding from the World Health Organization's cancer agency was more surprising, which is that very hot drinks, above about sixty-five degrees, probably cause cancer of the food pipe. Kofi, who had always drunk his tea scalding, set his mug down with great respect and waited for it to cool.

Amara found a small warning in her reading, which was that strong tea drunk with meals can block some of the iron from plant foods, a point that matters most to people who are already short of iron. Kofi added that nobody should drink strong tea late at night, since the caffeine in it would keep them awake. Health agencies, she noted, also advise against energy drinks for children, which often contain more caffeine than a cup of tea.

A yellow jar of turmeric stood beside a bowl of golden curry, and Kofi announced that this spice was the greatest superfood of all. Amara looked up curcumin, the main colourful substance in turmeric, and found hundreds of exciting laboratory studies in which it seemed to calm swollen cells and fight damage. She had learned to be suspicious of that exact pattern, because a dish of cells is a very long way from a living person.

The first problem with curcumin, Amara discovered, is that the body absorbs very little of it, although a pinch of black pepper helps a little. The second problem is that the trials in people are mostly small, short and uneven in quality, and they do not agree with each other. On her ladder, turmeric stood at the top of the laboratory rung and near the bottom of the trial rung.

Amara also found reports that high-dose turmeric pills have, in rare cases, been linked to liver problems, whereas the amounts used in cooking are generally regarded as safe. She told Kofi that nobody should take strong supplements without asking a doctor first, especially anyone already on medicine. Kofi dished out the golden curry with a flourish and said that it needed no health claim to justify its existence, because it tasted marvellous.

Amara broke a square of dark chocolate in two and held it to the light, because cocoa is rich in plant substances called flavanols. Small trials show that these substances may lower blood pressure slightly, though much of the flavanol content is lost when cocoa is heavily processed into a bar. Chocolate also carries sugar and fat, she reminded Kofi, so a square or two is a treat that does not need to be taken as medicine.

Amara and Zainab ran a small taste test in the classroom, with Zainab blindfolded and Amara handing over two pieces of chocolate in a random order decided by a coin. Zainab guessed correctly only half the time, and she admitted that when she could see the wrapper she had always been sure. The little experiment taught them why serious trials hide the answer, because people's opinions change when they know what they are eating.

Kofi opened a wooden spice box, and the little jars of ginger, cumin, black pepper and chilli released their smells into the room. Spices have no magic in them, he said, but they bring so much flavour that a cook can use less salt and sugar without anyone feeling cheated. Flavour is the secret ingredient of healthy eating, because people only keep eating the food that they enjoy.

Halfway through the eight weeks, Mrs Okoro read through Amara's notes with a pencil and asked what evidence would change her mind about turmeric. Amara replied without hesitation that a large, fair trial in people, with a clear result and honest reporting, would make her move it up the ladder at once. Her teacher put down the pencil and said that this answer was the mark of a real scientist.

Kofi tipped a bag of frozen peas into a pot in the middle of a busy afternoon, and he explained that he had relied on them throughout his restaurant years. Vegetables are usually frozen within hours of being picked, so they keep most of their vitamins, and nothing spoils in the freezer while you are waiting to cook. Amara was pleased to find that the research agreed with a cook's common sense.

Amara stacked tins of tomatoes, sweetcorn, beans and sardines on a pantry shelf and learned that canning preserves most of a food's nutrients, although some vitamin C is lost in the heat. Fruit should be tinned in juice and not syrup, beans and vegetables should be tinned without added salt, and a quick rinse of the beans gets rid of much of the salt that remains. A good tin, she decided, is a small treasure chest for a busy week.

Amara placed a limp lettuce that had lived in the fridge for a week beside a bag of frozen spinach, and the contrast was embarrassing for the lettuce. Fresh vegetables slowly lose some of their vitamins, especially vitamin C, as they sit for days in shops and kitchens. Fresh is wonderful when it is truly fresh, she concluded, but frozen and tinned are no second-class citizens.

Kofi handed Amara a small purse with a strict limit and challenged her to buy a week of healthy meals for the family at the market. Auntie Grace, who watched her counting coins with a smile, showed her how to compare prices, to buy what was plentiful, and to ask for the vegetables that were slightly bruised but perfectly good. By the end of the morning, Amara had learned more about money than about vitamins.

Amara's basket held a cabbage, a bag of dried beans, a box of oats and a bunch of carrots, and there was still money left in the purse. Eggs, tinned fish, frozen vegetables, bananas and even potatoes, which are a good source of potassium and vitamin C when eaten with the skin, belong on the same cheap and nutritious list. Healthy food, she realised, does not have to be rare, imported or expensive, and the best of it is often sitting on the cheapest shelf.

Kofi simmered vegetable peelings, stalks and old bones in a big pot to make stock, because in thirty years of cooking he had never been able to bear waste. Amara learned from the labels that a use by date is about safety and should be respected, while a best before date is about quality and food is often still fine afterwards. Wasting less food, she reflected, saves money and is kinder to the planet too.

At Auntie Grace's stall, a cart of pumpkins and tomatoes glowed in the late afternoon sun, and the prices on the cards had dropped. Produce that is in season is plentiful, so it costs less and often tastes better, and sellers are glad to lower their prices at the end of the day. Amara scribbled in her notebook that the cheapest vegetable is usually the one that the land is producing right now.

Kofi, who had passed many food inspections in his time, taught Amara the rules of the fridge, which put raw chicken on the bottom shelf where it cannot drip onto other food. Cooked rice, he warned, must be cooled quickly and refrigerated within an hour or so, because germs that survive cooking can multiply if it sits warm for hours. Safe food, Amara wrote on the poster, is the first requirement of healthy food, and no nutrient can make up for a stomach full of germs.

In a long supermarket queue, Amara watched a woman count her coins twice before she paid for a loaf of bread and a bag of rice. It struck her that advice about food can sound cruel if it ignores money, time, culture and the distance to the nearest fresh market. She wrote a new rule on her card, which said that good advice has to fit the person who receives it.

That evening, Amara and Kofi cooked a one-pot dinner of beans, vegetables and rice for six, and Amara worked out the cost for each person. Efua, who counted every coin in the household, was astonished at how small the number was, and Kojo ate three spoonfuls before he decided he was full. The Protection Plate, Amara noted, was beginning to look like a plan that real families could afford.

At school, Amara walked beside Zainab, who held a bright fizzy drink, while she herself carried a full water bottle. Water is the best everyday drink, since it contains no sugar, costs almost nothing from the tap, and quenches thirst better than anything else. Milk, tea and coffee can also play a part, Amara noted, as long as nobody pours half a bag of sugar into them.

Amara read the label on a can of fizzy drink and found that it often holds about thirty-five grams of sugar. She counted out nine level teaspoons into a glass, and Zainab, who had been drinking one a day, stared at the white pile in silence. Sometimes the most convincing experiment, Amara thought, is simply a spoon and a glass.

Too much sugar is strongly linked with tooth decay, and large studies also link sugary drinks with weight gain and type two diabetes. In a trial in the Netherlands, several hundred children were given either a sugary or a sugar-free drink each day for about eighteen months, and those given the sugary drink gained more fat. It was a fair trial with a clear result, and it earned the sugary drink a firm place on the wrong side of the plate.

The World Health Organization advises that free sugars, which means sugars added to food plus those in honey, syrups and fruit juice, should stay below ten percent of daily energy. For a typical adult diet that comes to about twelve teaspoons, and the guide adds that cutting the amount even further brings extra benefits. Amara translated the figures onto a measuring spoon and found that the limit is easy to pass without noticing.

Amara emptied the kitchen cupboard onto the table and read the labels on the ketchup, the breakfast cereal and the jars of sauce, finding sugar in nearly every one. It hides under many names, including glucose syrup, honey, cane sugar and fruit juice concentrate, and the ingredient list shows them in order of weight. Kofi, who had not looked at a label in thirty years, put on his reading glasses and said nothing for a long time.

Sugar-free drinks replace sugar with sweeteners, so they add no sugar to the diet, and many people find them a useful stepping stone. In 2023, however, the World Health Organization advised against relying on sweeteners to control weight, because the long-term evidence of benefit is weak. Kofi, who liked a sweet drink at wedding feasts, said that an occasional bottle was fine, and that water was still the honest answer.

Amara set a bowl of whole fruit beside a glass of juice and explained why they are not equal, because whole fruit keeps its fibre and slows the way sugar enters the blood. Juice and smoothies count as free sugars, and some national guides say that a small glass a day is the most that should count towards the daily five. Dried fruit, being sticky and concentrated, is best kept to a small handful and not eaten by the bagful.

At last Amara could return to the yellow note that said sugar makes children wild, which had been waiting on the fridge since the first week. Careful trials, in which neither the children nor their parents knew who had been given sugar, found no clear change in behaviour. Parents who believed their child had eaten sugar, however, did report a wilder child, so the noise at a party seems to come from the party.

Kofi sat at the table with a slice of birthday cake and a single candle, and he ate it very slowly, one forkful at a time. Treats can be part of a healthy life, Amara decided, provided they are special, shared and not an everyday habit. Feeling guilty about cake, she wrote, is not a health plan, and enjoyment is part of why people stay with a way of eating.

Amara went round her class with a clipboard, asked everyone what they usually drank at lunch, and counted the answers on a tally sheet. More than half of them chose a sugary drink, and she presented the figures to Mrs Okoro with a short list of facts about sugar and teeth. Her teacher listened carefully, nodded, and agreed that a water jug should go on every table in the canteen.

Beside a salt shaker on the counter, Kofi lined up fresh herbs and lemons, and Amara read out what the World Health Organization advises, which is less than five grams of salt a day, about one level teaspoon. The body does need a little sodium to work properly, but surveys show that many people eat about twice the recommended amount. Kofi looked at the shaker with the guilty face of a man who had used it very freely for thirty years.

At the clinic, a nurse showed Amara how a cuff measures blood pressure, wrapping it around Kofi's arm while the machine hummed and squeezed. In many people, a high-salt diet raises blood pressure over the years, and high blood pressure is a major risk factor for stroke and heart disease. Trials in which people eat less salt show that blood pressure falls, often within a few weeks, which makes this one of the clearest findings in the whole subject.

Amara drew a pie chart of the salt in an ordinary lunch of a sandwich, a bowl of soup and a sauce, and the sections for bread and soup were enormous. In many countries most of the salt that people eat comes from bread, soups, sauces and processed foods, and only a small part comes from the shaker on the table. Cutting back, she realised, is less about the shaker on the table than about the choices made in the shop and the kitchen.

Amara read the label on a loaf of bread and found more salt than she had expected from something so plain. Kofi, who had added stock cubes to nearly every pot in his restaurant, picked one up, read the tiny print, and went quiet for a moment. Salt on a label is often written as sodium, she told him, and the quick sum is to multiply the sodium by two and a half.

Kofi tasted his stew before reaching for the shaker for the first time in thirty years, and then he added lemon, fresh herbs and a pinch of chilli. Herbs, spices, citrus, vinegar and garlic can all carry flavour on their own, and many people find that their taste adjusts within a few weeks to the lighter touch. The trick, he decided, is to add salt in small amounts at the end and not in great handfuls at the beginning.

Amara learned that potassium, a mineral found in beans, greens, bananas and potatoes, may help to blunt the effect of salt on blood pressure. It is one more reason why the foods already on her plate work together, since many of them are low in salt and high in potassium at the same time. Nobody, she noted, should take potassium supplements without medical advice, because too much can be dangerous for some people.

In the clinic, Amara watched a doctor explain something quietly to an older patient, and she remembered that general advice is never the same as personal advice. Some people with certain conditions are told to eat even less salt than the usual guide, while a few others, with different conditions or on certain medicines, may need more. Her project could only describe what is true for most people, she wrote, and it could never tell any reader what is right for them.

Amara placed two tins of soup side by side and compared them using the column that shows the amount in every hundred grams, which is the fairest way to judge two foods of different sizes. One tin held almost twice as much salt as the other, even though the labels on the front looked equally cheerful. In some countries, she discovered, red, amber and green colours on the front of a pack help shoppers to see at a glance what is high and what is low.

Kofi sat alone at the kitchen table with a pot of his old restaurant stew, and he admitted to Amara that he had used far too much salt in thirty years of cooking. He had always cooked to make his customers come back, he said, and salt was the quickest way to make a dish taste like more. It was a brave thing to admit, and Amara hugged him, and told him that he had not known what the evidence now shows.

Amara cooked two pots of stew, one with plenty of salt and one with herbs, lemon and only a little salt, and she asked Efua and Zainab to taste both with their eyes closed. To her delight, Efua chose the lighter stew twice, and Zainab, who could not tell the pots apart on the second try, asked for the recipe. The Protection Plate gained a little corner of green herbs, with a small label that read, flavour without the shaker.

A tray of sausages and ham slices sat beside a plate of grilled vegetables, and Kofi, who loved a meat stew above all things, defended them loudly. Meat does provide protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12, Amara agreed, so the question is not whether meat is evil but which kinds of meat, and how much of them, a person eats. The answer, as usual, turned out to depend on the evidence, and Amara was determined to find it before the weekend was over.

In 2015, more than twenty experts from ten countries met at the cancer agency of the World Health Organization to review hundreds of studies on meat and cancer. Their job was to decide how strong the evidence was that eating certain meats can cause cancer, and not to say how big the danger is. Amara underlined that distinction twice, because it would matter a great deal in the next paragraph.

The panel placed processed meat, such as sausages, ham, bacon and salami, in Group One, the group for things where the evidence of cancer is strong, and this group also holds tobacco. The groups, however, measure how sure scientists are and not how large the risk is, so a sausage is not remotely as dangerous as a cigarette. The risk rises with the amount eaten, Amara noted, and for a person who eats a small amount occasionally it remains small.

Red meat, meaning beef, pork, lamb and goat, was placed one step lower, in Group Two A, because the evidence that it causes bowel cancer was judged to be limited rather than strong. Many health guides suggest keeping it to a few modest portions a week, and choosing fish, beans or poultry on the other days. Kofi stirred his beef stew thoughtfully and said that he would simply put in less beef and more of everything else.

Kofi made a new kind of stew, with a handful of beans for every slice of sausage, and he let the smoky meat flavour the whole pot. The stew tasted just as rich as his old recipe, and it cost less and carried far less processed meat. Small swaps like this, Amara wrote, are worth more than any dramatic ban, because people can keep them up for years.

Amara scrubbed a cutting board with hot soapy water after cutting raw chicken, while Kofi reminded her of the rules he had followed for thirty years. Raw chicken should never be washed, because the splashes spread germs across the sink and the counter, but it should be cooked all the way through until no pink remains. Poultry and fish are often better choices than red meat, she wrote, but only when they are handled safely.

A supermarket shelf was crowded with brightly wrapped snacks and ready meals, and Amara read the long ingredient lists on the back. Ultra-processed foods are made mostly from industrial ingredients that nobody would find in a home kitchen, such as flavour enhancers and modified starch, and researchers in Brazil proposed sorting foods by how much processing they receive. The label she looked for was a short list of ingredients that she could picture in a kitchen.

A small trial in 2019 gave Amara a rare example of fair evidence about processed food, in which twenty adults lived in a research centre for a month and ate two different diets. On the ultra-processed diet they ate about five hundred more calories a day than on the other and gained about a kilogram, even though both diets had been matched on the nutrients that were measured. The trial was short and small, Amara cautioned, but it suggested that something about these foods makes it easy to overeat.

Kofi held a slice of bread in one hand and a ready meal tray in the other, and he pointed out that bread, tinned beans, frozen peas, yoghurt and cheese are all processed in some way. Scientists admit that the line between helpful and unhelpful processing is blurry, and they still argue about how best to define it. A good rule, Amara decided, is to favour foods with short ingredient lists, and not to be frightened of anything that comes in a tin.

Efua came home late from a long day at work, kicked off her shoes, and heated a ready meal for the family while Amara set the table. Amara noticed that her mother looked tired rather than guilty, and she realised that a project about food must never make people ashamed of the way they manage busy lives. The best diet, she wrote, is the one that a real person can keep, with all the tiredness, the budget and the clock that real life brings.

At a family dinner, Amara looked at a glass of water and a glass of wine standing side by side, and wondered which one a scientist would choose. Alcohol is classed by the World Health Organization's cancer agency as a cause of cancer, and it raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, liver, bowel and breast. She wrote the facts without any lecture, because the evidence is strong enough to speak for itself.

An old newspaper clipping claimed that a glass of red wine each day would help people to live longer, and for years the claim was repeated at dinner tables. Later researchers noticed a flaw, which was that the people who did not drink often included former drinkers who had quit because they were already ill, so the drinkers looked healthier by comparison. It was a perfect example of the traps Amara had learned about in the first weeks of her project, and she smiled.

The World Health Organization has said plainly that no level of alcohol is completely safe for health, and that the risk rises as the amount increases. Young people, whose bodies are still developing, and women who are pregnant are advised not to drink at all, and many medicines do not mix with alcohol. Amara did not put alcohol anywhere on her plate, while Kofi, who liked a small glass at weddings, listened with respect and said nothing.

Kofi lifted blackened toast from the grill and waved away the smoke, and the smoke alarm joined in loudly. When starchy foods such as toast, chips and roast potatoes are cooked until they are dark brown, a chemical called acrylamide forms, and in animal studies it can cause cancer. Some food agencies therefore advise cooking these foods to a golden yellow, and Amara copied the rule onto her poster in big letters.

At a neighbour's barbecue, Amara watched the meat darken over flames, and she remembered that cooking meat at very high heat creates compounds that damage cells in laboratory tests. Evidence from studies of people is mixed, so she did not claim that a barbecue is dangerous, but the sensible advice is easy to follow. Cook gently, cut off blackened parts, turn the meat often, and consider a marinade, since some studies suggest that it may reduce these compounds.

Kofi showed Amara a deep pot of dark oil like the kind he used to reuse for days in his restaurant, and he confessed that he would not do it now. Oil that is heated again and again breaks down, smokes and develops harmful substances, so fresh oil is better, and it should never be heated until it is smoking. Baking, steaming and stir-frying with a small amount of oil, she wrote, are usually kinder to both the food and the cook.

Amara found a lesson in the corner of Kofi's storeroom, where a sealed tin kept the groundnuts dry and away from damp air. Moulds that grow on stored groundnuts, maize and other grains can make poisons called aflatoxins, which are linked with liver cancer and with poor growth in children. Dry storage, good sorting and throwing away anything mouldy or shrivelled are simple habits that protect whole communities, she wrote.

Amara lined up four pans on the stove, labelled steam, boil, bake and stir fry, and drew up a table of what each method does to flavour, vitamins and fat. Steaming keeps the most vitamins, boiling is simple but wastes the water, baking brings out sweetness, and stir frying uses a little oil to carry flavour. No method wins every contest, she concluded, so the best one is whichever keeps a person eating vegetables.

Amara drew a Safer Kitchen poster for her display board, with small pictures of hand washing, a cold fridge, a thermometer, golden toast and a sealed tin of nuts. She wrote beneath each picture a single rule that she had learned in the last few weeks, from the way to cook chicken to the way to store rice. Kofi pinned a copy above his own cooker, and joked that it was about thirty years too late for his restaurant.

At the end of the sixth week, Amara drew a second ring on her Protection Plate, a small corner that she labelled keep small. It held salt, sugar, processed meat and alcohol, which are not forbidden foods but foods where the evidence says that less is better. The plate now had two halves to its story, what to add and what to ease off, and she thought it looked a lot more honest.

Amara opened a kitchen cupboard and found it stuffed with bottles of vitamin pills that Kofi had bought over the years because of advertisements. She explained that a pill holds a handful of isolated nutrients, whereas a plate of food holds thousands of substances working together, along with fibre and water. Kofi looked at the bottles and said that he had paid a great deal for a very small part of a carrot.

Amara studied a row of trial results and saw a pattern that was quite different from the one for whole foods. Many large trials had given vitamin and mineral pills to healthy people for years, and mostly they found no clear protection against heart disease or cancer. A pill, it seemed, cannot do the work of a plate, and she placed a firm question mark on the whole supplement shelf.

In the 1990s, two big trials, one in Finland and one in the United States, gave high-dose beta-carotene pills to people at high risk of lung cancer, most of them smokers. The researchers expected the pills to protect, because people who ate plenty of beta-carotene-rich vegetables had less cancer, but there was more lung cancer in the groups taking pills. One of the trials was stopped early, and the lesson, Amara wrote, is that a substance that is good inside a vegetable may be harmful when swallowed in large amounts.

Amara drew a bottle of vitamin A capsules next to a bunch of carrots with a warning triangle between them, because the two are very different. Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and can build up in the body, and very large doses of vitamin A can cause harm, especially to an unborn baby. Excess from ordinary food is unusual, she noted, whereas excess from pills is easy and deserves respect.

Amara took her list of questions to the local clinic and interviewed Ms Adebayo, a registered dietitian who had spent years helping people with food and health. Ms Adebayo explained that her title is protected, because she has trained for years and is regulated, whereas in many places anyone at all can call themselves a nutritionist. Amara wrote down the lesson at once, which was to check who is giving the advice as well as what they say.

Ms Adebayo pointed to a colourful chart on the clinic wall and told Amara that most healthy people who eat a varied diet do not need vitamin pills. She was careful to add that this was a general statement, and that in her own work she always looks at the individual person, their health, their medicines and their diet, before she suggests anything. Amara realised that she had just watched a professional do exactly what her teacher had always asked, which was to admit the limits of what she knew.

Outside the clinic window, a thin winter sun shone on the street, and Ms Adebayo used it to explain that the skin makes vitamin D when sunlight touches it. People who spend little time outdoors, or who live far from the equator, can run low in the darker months, and some national guides advise supplements at those times. A doctor can test for it, she said, which is far better than guessing.

Ms Adebayo warned that the word natural is not a promise of safety, because some natural foods and herbs can change the way medicines work in the body. Grapefruit can interfere with several common medicines, and the herb St John's wort can weaken others, including some contraceptive pills. Anyone who takes medicine, she repeated, should ask a pharmacist before adding any herb, supplement or unusual food to their daily routine.

A tub of immune booster powder promised to make the body stronger against every germ, and Amara read the label with a raised eyebrow. A healthy immune system is a balance, not a muscle that grows bigger with exercise, and one that is overactive can cause problems such as allergies. There is no good evidence that a powder can safely boost it, she wrote, whereas sleep, vaccines, movement and a varied diet help it to do its normal job.

Dev, a classmate whose project was about supplements, stood at a table lined with bottles and argued with Amara in the friendliest possible way. She showed him her ladder, he showed her a list of vitamins that some people really do need, and they discovered that they agreed on more than either had expected. Both of them shook hands on the one rule that mattered, which was to keep asking where the evidence comes from.

Amara held up a bag of crisps wrapped in a golden banner that proclaimed the contents a superfood, because the crisps were made from beetroot. She had learned that the word has no scientific definition, and that it is chosen by marketers because it makes people feel hopeful and reach for their purses. A vegetable crisp, she noted, is still mainly salt and oil, and a hopeful word does not change its ingredients.

A bottle of detox tea promised to flush poisons from the body in three days, and it carried a picture of a glowing liver. Amara explained that the liver and kidneys already clear waste around the clock, and that no clear scientific evidence shows that detox diets do anything extra. Some of these products contain strong laxatives that can cause real harm, and among the best things for the liver is simply to drink little alcohol and eat a varied diet.

Amara placed a packet of low-fat biscuits beside a box of cereal marked no added sugar, and she read both labels line by line. Foods that have lost their fat often gain extra sugar to replace the flavour, while the words no added sugar do not mean there is no sugar, since fruit and juices carry their own. Marketing words, she realised, describe what is missing from a food and say very little about what is in it.

In a neat row on a shelf stood packets marked natural, organic and gluten free, and Amara asked what each word really promised. Organic describes the way food is grown, natural has almost no fixed meaning, and gluten free is essential for people with coeliac disease but is no healthier for people without it. None of these words, she wrote, can replace the question of what is actually inside the packet.

Amara read the back of a cereal box with her magnifying glass, and Kofi leaned over her shoulder to see what she had found. Ingredients are listed in order of weight, so the first item is the biggest part of the food, and the maker chooses the portion size, which is often smaller than what people really pour. The first three ingredients, Amara said, tell you most of what you need to know about a packet.

Amara drew a table in pencil and compared two cereals line by line, with sugar, fibre and salt per hundred grams side by side. The cereal with the cheerful cartoon on the front had nearly three times as much sugar and about half the fibre of the plain one with the dull box. Kofi squinted through his reading glasses at the tiny print and muttered that in his day a cereal was just a cereal.

In some places, including the European Union, a claim such as “helps lower cholesterol” may only appear on a pack after experts have reviewed the evidence and approved it. Amara found the oat claim on the list, and smiled to see an old friend from her fourth week, but she also found a long list of claims that had been rejected for lack of proof. A rule that makes the claim face the evidence, she decided, is a rule worth having.

Amara watched a glossy video in which a famous wellness influencer promised that one special powder would transform anyone's health. She paused it and asked her questions, which were who is saying this, how many people were studied, what kind of study it was, and who is being paid. The influencer, she discovered, owned the company that sold the powder, and the only evidence on offer was a collection of happy customers.

Kofi stuck two old headlines side by side on the fridge, one saying that eggs are bad for you and the other saying that eggs are good for you. Science does move forward, and new studies can change the details, but the basic advice about eating mostly plants, less salt and less sugar has stayed remarkably steady for decades. Much of the whiplash, Amara concluded, is made by headlines that need to be exciting, and not by scientists who change their minds every week.

Mrs Okoro read through the whole file and told Amara that her project had quietly changed from a list of foods into a way of deciding what to believe. Amara agreed, and she made a poster called Five Questions About Any Food Claim, which asked who says it, how many people were studied, what kind of study it was, how big the effect is, and who gains. Kofi stuck it to the fridge, where it stayed for the rest of the year.

Amara jogged beside Kofi along a park path at sunset, though Kofi, whose knees complained loudly, soon decided that walking fast was a better idea. The World Health Organization suggests at least an hour of moderate or vigorous activity a day for young people and at least two and a half hours a week for adults. Movement, Amara realised, was the missing partner of her plate, because food alone had never been the whole story of health.

In the park, Amara's friends played football while Kofi walked slowly around the edge of the pitch, and Amara realised that they were all doing something good for their health. Regular physical activity is among the best-supported habits of all, with evidence from large studies and from trials showing benefits for the heart, the bones, mood and sleep. Any movement counts, she decided, from football to dancing to a brisk walk to the market, and the best kind is the kind that a person enjoys.

After a late night of homework, Amara dragged herself to school and ate three biscuits before the first lesson, which gave her an idea for her project. Teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep, and small trials suggest that people who are short of sleep feel hungrier and are drawn towards sugary and fatty foods. Sleep, she wrote, is not food, but it quietly shapes what people choose to eat.

Kofi found an old cigarette lighter at the back of a drawer, held it above the bin for a moment, and told Amara that he had stopped smoking twenty years ago. Smoking is the largest cause of preventable cancer and early death in many countries, and no diet, however perfect, can undo the harm that it does. Quitting, he said, was the best thing he had ever done, and the sooner a person stops, the more of the harm the body can repair.

One afternoon, Amara sat at a quiet kitchen table with Efua and talked about the link between food and mood. Some small trials suggest that improving a poor diet may lift mood a little, and that regular meals help people to feel steadier, but the evidence is early. Food is not a treatment for depression, she wrote, and anyone who feels low for a long time should talk to a doctor or another trusted adult.

On Sunday the whole family gathered around one table, with Amara, Kofi, a cousin and two friends all laughing and passing dishes. Studies link shared meals with healthier eating among children and teenagers, though families who eat together may differ in other ways, so this is a clue and not proof. Whatever the science says, Amara noticed, a meal shared with people you love tends to be slower, happier and much more memorable.

Kofi cooked his mother's famous stew beneath her framed portrait on the kitchen wall, and the smell carried him back sixty years to his own childhood. Food is not only a set of nutrients, Amara understood, because it carries culture, memory and love from one generation to the next. The sensible way to improve a favourite dish, she wrote, is to adapt it with more vegetables, beans or herbs and less salt, instead of abandoning it.

Mrs Okoro rested a hand on Amara's desk and reminded her that a project about food should never make anyone afraid of eating. Some people begin by wanting to eat well and end by worrying about every bite, and for them it can become a serious illness that needs real help. If thoughts about food ever take over, Amara added to her poster, the right step is to talk to a trusted adult or a doctor.

Amara and Kofi decided to try an experiment at supper, in which they put their forks down between bites and noticed how hungry they still felt. The body takes a little while to signal that it has had enough, so eating slowly gives those signals time to arrive, and it also lets a person taste the food. Listening to hunger and fullness, she wrote, is a skill that children have and many adults forget.

On Sunday evening Amara watched the sun go down after a day with a long walk, a lunch with the family and some honest homework, and she felt pleasantly tired. Nothing she had done that day was perfect, but all of it was good enough, and good enough repeated for years is what the evidence rewards. Health, she wrote, is a pattern of days, and not one perfect plate, and she was glad that she had finally understood it.

In his high chair, Amara's little brother Kojo, who was two years old, pushed a spoonful of green beans away with the tip of one finger and a look of deep disgust. Efua sighed, because it was the sixth night that he had refused them, and she wondered aloud whether she was doing something wrong. Amara, who now had a whole file on evidence, realised that for once she had a useful answer.

Amara explained that young children often need to try a new food ten times or more before they accept it, and that refusing it is a normal stage and not a failure. Pressure, bribes and promises of dessert usually make the problem worse, whereas small portions, patience and parents who eat the food happily themselves tend to work better. A week later Kojo licked a single green bean, and Efua smiled as though he had won a prize, though she knew that a doctor is the one to ask if a child's eating worries her.

Kofi, now past seventy, ate slowly from a small bowl of stew and admitted that his appetite was not what it had been. Older adults often eat less, so each mouthful has to count, and they still need enough protein and nutrients to keep their muscles and bones strong. Amara added a note to her project that older people should ask a doctor or dietitian about vitamin D and vitamin B12, because needs change with age.

Amara stood at the stove with a wooden spoon while Efua read a recipe aloud from her phone, and for once the two of them were cooking as a team. Cooking at home from simple ingredients gives a person control over the salt, the sugar and the fat, and it costs less than most ready meals. It is also a skill, Amara realised, and like any skill it improves with practice and a little patience.

Kofi supervised from a chair while Amara made her first full pot of orange lentil soup, frying the onions gently, adding carrots and lentils, and then letting everything simmer until it was soft. Taste as you go, he told her, because a recipe is only a map and the cook has to walk the road. At the end she squeezed in a little lemon, and the whole family agreed that it was the best thing she had ever made.

With a ruler and her best coloured pens, Amara drew the final Protection Plate, half of it filled with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with whole grains and a quarter with protein such as beans, fish, eggs or poultry. Beside the plate she drew a glass of water and a spoon of plant oil, and in one corner she kept the small ring for salt, sugar, processed meat and alcohol. It looked almost like any healthy eating plate, she thought, except that every part of it had been checked against the evidence.

Amara asked her family to try the Protection Plate for seven days, and she kept a chart with a tick for each meal and a note about what happened. She knew perfectly well that one family trying one plate for one week is not a trial, since there is no comparison group, no chance and far too little time. What it could measure was cost, taste and how easy it felt, and she promised herself to claim nothing more.

On the fourth evening, the fridge was almost empty, Efua was exhausted and the whole plan seemed to be falling apart. Amara pulled a bag of frozen peas from the freezer, cracked some eggs into a pan with rice, and had a good, quick dinner on the table in fifteen minutes. A plan that cannot survive a bad day, she wrote in her notebook, is not a plan for real people, so she added frozen vegetables to the list of rescues.

At the end of the week the family sat around the table with the diary and counted the ticks, and the results were modest but real. The meals had cost a little less, Kojo had eaten more vegetables than before, and Efua said that cooking had felt calmer once the plan was clear. Nobody could say whether anyone was healthier after a single week, Amara wrote, because that is simply not something a week can show.

Amara and Kofi sat over the final report with a pencil and cups of tea, correcting commas and checking every number against its source. At the end she added a section called What We Do Not Know, which listed the many questions that the evidence had left open, from probiotics to turmeric to the best amount of fish. Kofi read the last page twice, and said that he had never read anything that was so honest and so useful at the same time.

On the morning of the Science Fair, the school hall filled with the smell of floor polish and the sound of scraping chairs, and Amara set up her display board with trembling hands. Her Evidence Ladder stood at the centre, the Protection Plate was pinned beside it, and the Five Questions poster hung proudly on the right. Kofi arrived early in his best shirt with a basket of real food for the table, and told her that he had never been so nervous, not even on opening night at the restaurant.

Dev's board about supplements stood on one side of Amara's and Zainab's project about water on the other, and visitors wandered happily between all three. A small girl stopped at the ladder, and Amara explained it as a game in which stories are on the floor and trials are near the ceiling, and the child nodded gravely. If a child could grasp it in a minute, Amara thought, the idea was probably worth the eight weeks it had taken.

A parent leaned in and asked Amara the question that every visitor wanted to ask, which was simply what people should eat. Amara answered that no single food holds the secret, and that the evidence points to a pattern with plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains and fish, a little less salt, sugar and processed meat, and meals that people enjoy. She added, carefully, that she could only describe what is true for most people, and that anyone with a health condition should ask a doctor or dietitian.

A visitor held up a bottle of a miracle product that she had bought online and asked Amara whether it worked. Amara pointed to the poster and went through the five questions with her, and when they ran out of answers she said honestly that she did not know. Saying I do not know, she added with a smile, is not a failure in science, and it is where every good investigation starts.

Dr Mensah, a visiting nutrition researcher with a clipboard and a kind face, stopped at Amara's board with Mrs Okoro and asked whether these foods can prevent disease. Amara took a breath and answered that they may lower the risk of some diseases, as part of a whole pattern of eating, but that no food can guarantee anything because the body does the protecting and food only helps. The judge looked at Mrs Okoro and wrote something down, and Amara could not tell what it was.

The judge asked what she would do differently if she could start again, and Amara pointed to the section of her board headed Limits. She said that she would try a larger and fairer test with a comparison group and much more time, and that she would ask more experts to check her work. Dr Mensah's face softened, and he wrote a longer note than before, nodding slowly as if he had already made up his mind.

While the judges argued behind a closed door, Kofi and Amara sat on a bench in the corridor and ate sandwiches of bread, egg and tomato. Kofi said that he had learned more about food in eight weeks than in thirty years of cooking it, and that what surprised him most was how much he did not know. Amara said that she had learned the same thing about herself, and they clinked their sandwiches together like glasses.

Mrs Okoro announced the Honest Science Prize in front of the whole school, and when she read Amara's name the hall burst into applause. Outside, on the school steps at sunset, Kofi and Amara held the small trophy between them while Efua took photographs and Kojo tried to eat the ribbon. The judges, Mrs Okoro said later, had liked the project most because it was brave enough to say what it did not know.

Back at home, Kofi opened a new notebook, wrote a title at the top of the first page, and asked if he could join Amara's next project. They agreed to make a family cookbook of favourite dishes, each one a little lighter on salt and a little heavier on vegetables, and each one tested on Kojo. The old restaurant notebook sat beside it, and Amara noticed that its last page had a note in Kofi's handwriting that said, show the evidence.

That evening, Amara and Kofi ate a simple supper of beans, vegetables and rice on the doorstep, and agreed that the project had changed how they thought about food more than how they cooked it.
